lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.

lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But beliefs do shift a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.

lines.short: Maybe the visual brain's own wiring. A maths model shows how tunnels, spirals, cobwebs and honeycombs could arise there. It wasn't tested in people on a drug.
lines.but: It's only maths: the drug is just a setting for how excitable the brain is. The match was judged by eye against a few drawings.
how: People see simple shapes after LSD or cannabis. They also come with flickering light or when falling asleep. Long ago, these were sorted into four types: lattices and honeycombs, cobwebs, tunnels, and spirals.
The wiring from eye to brain turns a tunnel or a spiral into plain stripes. These run across the brain's first area for sight.
In the model, when that area gets too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form by themselves, shaped by how its cells connect. Mapped back to what you'd see, they look like all four types.
The wiring data came mostly from cats and monkeys. The best matches needed wider connections than that anatomy shows, and some complex visions don't fit the model.

lines.short: Desire often goes up, erections can go either way, and orgasm often takes longer. In one survey, 8 of 20 men said erections got weaker on MDMA, and 8 stronger.
lines.but: It's 35 people who chose to talk about it, remembering past experiences. Nobody tested their pills.
how: In Israel, 20 men and 15 women who had used MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex. All 35 said desire went up, and 32 said they were more satisfied.
Of the 20 men, 8 said erections got weaker and 8 stronger. Orgasm took longer for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 3 people couldn't reach it, yet still felt more satisfied.
In Northern Ireland, 98 people were interviewed. A little over half said MDMA was more about closeness than sex. Some men couldn't get an erection; others described strong desire.
Some described one-night stands and regret. Condoms were rare on ecstasy, but also rare without drugs, so the study can't show MDMA made sex riskier.

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.

The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water. In one study, 8 healthy men given one MDMA capsule had a rise in the water-holding hormone, and their blood salt fell a little, not to a low level. It had no proper comparison, and a study of 32 people found no clear rise in a related marker.

Heart rate rose about 20 beats a minute after MDA and 31 after MDMA, though the paper calls them similar. Top blood pressure rose about 30 points with both.

lines.short: Mostly how long it lasts: about 9 to 11 hours for LSD, 6 to 7 for psilocybin, the drug in mushrooms. Otherwise 28 people in a lab rated the trips alike.
lines.but: Finding no difference in 28 people doesn't prove there is none. And most could tell which drug they'd had.
how: 28 healthy adults each had five hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got a dummy, two amounts of LSD and two of psilocybin, in random order, not told which.
LSD lasted longer at both amounts. It also began a bit sooner, which the authors put down to it being a liquid, not a capsule.
The higher psilocybin amount raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more. LSD raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints like headaches; nobody had a serious problem.
By the study's own figures, people named the right drug in most sessions, which may have shaped their ratings. It used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms.

how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound. They can feel like the problem the pills were for, and sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep even after a few nights.
Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen with slow tapering, but calls most reports anecdotes; the other cites no source.
The only count: in 1961, 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

card.statement: Two expert reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos suddenly say how often they happen.
card.why: Both warn the seizures can be life-threatening, but neither gives a rate. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners in 1961, in conditions unlike usual use.

lines.short: Partly: people feel warmer, but they don't read others better. In a lab test, they named 55 in 100 fearful faces correctly on MDMA, against 63 on a dummy pill.
lines.but: These were small lab studies. People rated photos and played a money game instead of talking with real people.
how: 21 people who had used ecstasy took MDMA, meth or a dummy pill on different days. MDMA raised 'loving' and 'friendly' ratings over the dummy pill, but not clearly over meth. Only meth clearly raised 'sociable'.

In the same study, faces flashed up for half a second. People named 55 in 100 fearful faces right on MDMA, against 63 on the dummy pill. An earlier study of 9 people, who rated clear faces as pleasant, neutral or unpleasant, found no significant change.

In Basel, 32 healthy people felt a bit more for people in photos on MDMA (about 5.0 against 4.4 out of 9), but got worse at naming fear, anger, disgust and surprise. Oxytocin rose, but didn't match these changes.
In a money game with real payouts, people more often picked the split that gave the other person the most. Most volunteers could tell they'd had MDMA, and many tests were run.

card.statement: MDMA helps you tell what other people feel.
card.why: In lab tests, people felt warmer on MDMA but didn't read others better, and they named fear correctly less often. These were small studies using photos.

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

card.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked a single psilocybin session among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
card.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

items.what: a limit of one trial moved onto another

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

card.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear after 12 weeks.
card.why: By 12 weeks, the gap with the comparison group could be chance. People could probably tell they'd taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the earlier gap look bigger.

lines.short: People who use cannabis, most of all daily, get psychosis more often than people who don't.
lines.but: This is a link: these studies cannot show that cannabis was the cause.
how: Seven big studies followed young people for years. Those who had ever used cannabis had about 1.4 times the odds of psychosis later, mostly symptoms rather than a diagnosed illness, compared with people who never had.

For each study's heaviest-use group (from more than 50 times to daily use or dependence), the odds were about twice as high. In two studies of people with a first psychosis, daily use went with about 3 times the odds, and using now and then was not linked.

In a big Swedish study of men, about 6 in 1,000 who had never used cannabis, and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times, later went to hospital with schizophrenia. These counts do not allow for other differences between the men.
Taking other differences between people into account, such as other drug use and other mental health problems, shrank the link by about half.

card.statement: Most men who used cannabis heavily never went to hospital with schizophrenia, in a big Swedish study.
card.why: About 38 in 1,000 men who'd used it more than 50 times later did, against about 6 in 1,000 who had never used it. These counts don't allow for other differences between the men.

lines.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
lines.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

card.statement: Teen cannabis use has been shown to lower IQ later in life.
card.why: Not shown either way: in one New Zealand study, people dependent on cannabis for years lost about 6 IQ points, but other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of mostly lighter teenage use found no clear extra loss, though they could miss a small one.

lines.short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.
lines.but: These are computer estimates built on studies of groups of people, not counted deaths.
how: The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women.
At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study: about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.
An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, mostly from injuries, heart disease, cancer and cirrhosis, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented.
A later round of the global study, quoted second-hand, put it at about 1.8 million in 2020. The numbers move with the method, so they do not show a trend.

card.statement: Worldwide, alcohol is estimated to cause millions of deaths a year.
card.why: Global models put it at about 2.3 to 2.8 million a year, against a world where no one drank, and at ages 15 to 49 it was the top risk factor in one study. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

lines.short: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of the serotonin marker.
lines.but: The amounts come from memory, and people who take more ecstasy take more of everything else.
how: Four studies found this link; two smaller ones did not.
In one, each doubling of pills went with a small further drop.
In another, years of use and the biggest dose went with the lowest levels.
Nobody measured how much people really took, or what was in the pills.

card.statement: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of a serotonin marker, in most studies.
card.why: Four studies found this link and two smaller ones didn't. But amounts came from memory, and people who take more ecstasy also take more of other drugs.

lines.short: The good feelings fade within one dose and within three days; hunger stays gone.
lines.but: All of this used small oral doses in six to nine people in a laboratory.
how: Within one dose, the effects peak in about a quarter of an hour, then fade.
Over three days of twice-daily doses, the good feelings were gone by day three.
Eating stayed down over the three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew.
The body did not clear the drug faster; that was measured and had not changed.

card.statement: When meth's good feelings fade over days of use, the bad effects fade too.
card.why: In a small lab study, the good feelings were gone within three days, while dizziness, sickness and a pounding heart grew and appetite stayed down. Only six to nine people took part, on small doses.

lines.short: Yes: more people finished withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine.
lines.but: No trial reported people coming off fentanyl, and two stopped early, which may have skewed the results.
how: Fourteen trials put people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, on buprenorphine or on clonidine or lofexidine, by chance.
About 72 in 100 finished treatment on buprenorphine, against about 45 in 100 on the other medicines.
On buprenorphine, withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed in treatment longer than on the other medicines.
There was no clear difference in how many had side effects, but they differed: headache with buprenorphine, dizziness and dry mouth with clonidine.

card.statement: More people finish opioid withdrawal treatment on buprenorphine than on clonidine or lofexidine.
card.why: In 14 trials, about 72 in 100 finished on buprenorphine, against about 45 on the other medicines, and withdrawal was milder on average. No trial reported people coming off fentanyl.

lines.short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.
lines.but: These numbers are second-hand, from a 2022 review of single trials with 16 healthy people each.
how: Duloxetine and reboxetine lowered MDMA's rated effects. The MDMA peak in the blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher.
Bupropion did not lower the ratings. The MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak, 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less.

Some people feel little from an amount and take more. A slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ or a muting medicine can each be the reason. No trial tested what happened then.
The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion with MDMA might raise the chance of seizures.

card.statement: If an antidepressant mutes MDMA's effects, that means less MDMA is in your blood.
card.why: In small trials, two antidepressants lowered how strongly people rated MDMA's effects, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 15 to 18 percent higher. That's second-hand, from single trials of 16 healthy people each.

lines.short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.
lines.but: Voluntary reports cannot show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.
how: In 946 US reports about ecstasy, those that also named an antidepressant had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome.
Reports naming other kinds of medicine had higher odds still: about 8 times for muscle relaxants and about 7 times for anesthetics.
In a survey of 216 adults, 76 in 100 who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria. They also reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness.
The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.

card.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, cases that also named an antidepressant more often ended in death.
card.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

items.what: a finding in emergency patients said of everyone

lines.short: People who took GHB with alcohol were less awake more often at hospital.
lines.but: Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts were not known.
how: In 609 emergency patients who took GHB or GBL, 59 in 100 of those who also had alcohol were less awake, against 49 in 100 of those who did not. People who took other drugs were left out. Less awake means a Glasgow Coma Score under 13.
Of those kept in hospital, 55 in 100 with alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Across all patients, that is about 20 and 8 in 100.

Slow breathing (8 in 100 with alcohol, 12 without), breathing tubes (6 in 100 with alcohol, 4 without) and discharge did not clearly differ, but the study could not rule out a difference. Two people died, both with alcohol.
In 16 healthy volunteers, blood oxygen fell 2.1 points with both drugs, more than with either alone. That is a different measure from the patient study.

card.statement: People who took GHB or GBL with alcohol more often ended up in critical care than those without.
card.why: Of emergency patients kept in hospital, 55 in 100 who'd also had alcohol went to critical care, against 22 in 100 without. Alcohol use was reported, not measured, and the amounts weren't known.

lines.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
lines.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.

card.statement: In one study, people off heavy cannabis use for a year or more scored like people who hadn't used.
card.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

lines.short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.
lines.but: Nobody has measured real touches, and finding no proven case is not proof it never happens.
how: Poison experts did sums from fentanyl skin patches, made to deliver it. Powder on skin, they argue, is taken up more slowly and can be washed off.
Researchers checked 214 news stories about police or paramedics exposed to opioids. Only one incident mentioned any test, probably one that misses fentanyl.
A federal safety agency looked into three cases where seven officers felt ill. It found no signs of a serious overdose. No officer had a test that finds fentanyl.
Splashes into the eyes or mouth are treated as a real risk. No sums were done for carfentanil, far stronger than morphine in animals.

card.statement: Police officers have had confirmed overdoses from just touching fentanyl.
card.why: None has been confirmed: a federal safety agency looked into cases where officers felt ill and found no signs of a serious overdose, though no officer had a test that finds fentanyl. Finding no proven case isn't proof it never happens.

lines.short: Next morning, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly than a dummy dose.
lines.but: Memory tests showed no change, but the study was small and printed no test results.
how: Eleven people took a dummy dose and real doses on different days in a hospital unit.
Next morning they rated their mood and did memory and attention tests.
After the biggest dose, their heart beat faster and blood pressure was higher than after the dummy dose.
They did not feel sadder or more worried, or want meth more.

card.statement: One dose of meth leaves people sadder and craving it the next morning.
card.why: In one small lab study, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly the next morning than a dummy dose, but not sadder or more worried, and they didn't want meth more. Only eleven people took part, in a hospital unit.

lines.short: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths. Compared with people who never drank, there was no clear difference.
lines.but: Few studies made that comparison. So a small gain or a small loss is still possible.
how: Researchers put together dozens of studies. These followed millions of people for years and counted who died.
In most studies, the non-drinkers included people who had stopped drinking, some perhaps because they were ill. People who had stopped died more often.
Six studies started with younger people and compared them with people who had never drunk. There, people who drank a little died about as often.
Allowing for how the studies differed also shrank the gap. Researchers still disagree, and studies like these cannot show whether alcohol itself helps or harms.

card.statement: Studies show people who drink a little live longer than people who never drank.
card.why: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths in people who drink a little, but compared with people who had never drunk, there was no clear difference. Few studies made that comparison, so a small gain or a small loss is still possible.

lines.short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
lines.but: For small amounts it is less clear: older studies found slightly fewer strokes, but the Chinese gene study did not.
how: In a study of more than 160,000 Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes. The risk rose steadily with the amount.
For each extra 100 grams of alcohol a week (about 14 grams a day), bleeding strokes were almost a fifth more common, and strokes from blocked vessels about a tenth more common.
Women in China, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes. Most gene studies of people of European descent found the same direction.
Older studies comparing people who drink with people who don't found more strokes at high amounts, but no difference overall.

card.statement: In gene studies, drinking more went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.
card.why: In a big study of Chinese adults, men whose genes made them drink more had more strokes, and bleeding strokes rose most. Women, who mostly don't drink, showed no link with the same genes.

lines.short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.
lines.but: Neither study could rule out that early dementia, which can bring worry and poor sleep, led to the prescriptions.
how: In Quebec records, 50 in 100 older people with Alzheimer's had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years before, against 40 in 100 without it.
The link appeared only with longer use. The records often missed why the pills were taken, and held nothing on education, smoking or drinking.
A Seattle study tested 3,434 older people every 2 years. About 3 in 100 a year got dementia, with the heaviest use or none.
A small extra risk showed up with light or moderate use, not the heaviest. The authors say early dementia symptoms may explain it.

card.statement: Early dementia can itself lead to benzodiazepine prescriptions.
card.why: Worry and poor sleep can come before dementia and lead to these prescriptions, and neither of two big studies could rule that out. In one, the authors said early symptoms may explain a small extra risk with light or moderate use.

lines.short: An animal worm medicine often found in cocaine, linked to blood and skin harm.
lines.but: This comes from case reports, so how often it causes harm is unknown.
how: Around 2010 it was in about 7 in 10 cocaine samples tested by US drug police, and in 8 or 9 in 10 urine samples that tested positive for cocaine in two US cities.
In some people the white blood cells that fight infection fell very low. Counts came back 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or sooner with a hospital medicine.
Others had painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks or nose. Most healed within weeks of stopping cocaine, but some needed skin grafts or amputation.
Cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person used cocaine. Since most cocaine held it, finding it shows a person was exposed, not that it caused the harm.

card.statement: Levamisole, an animal worm medicine often found in cocaine around 2010, has been linked to blood and skin harm.
card.why: Case reports describe infection-fighting white blood cells falling very low, and painful purple skin patches, sometimes with dying skin. But since most cocaine held it, finding it shows exposure, not that it caused the harm, and how often harm happens is unknown.

lines.short: In two big trials, esketamine spray (a form of ketamine) did a little better than a dummy spray. Only one trial passed its main test.
lines.but: About 1 in 4 felt detached or unreal on esketamine, so many may have known which spray they got, and nobody asked.
how: In two trials, adults whose depression had not lifted on two antidepressants got esketamine or a dummy spray. All started a new antidepressant.
After 4 weeks, depression scores fell about 3 to 4 points more out of 60 with esketamine. A fast start was not shown.
Among people whose depression had lifted, 45 in 100 switched to a dummy spray relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine.
The company behind it paid for every trial. Two critics argue relapses may partly be effects of stopping; the trial could not tell.

card.statement: People whose depression lifted on esketamine relapsed more often when switched to a dummy spray.
card.why: Of those switched to a dummy spray, 45 in 100 relapsed, against 27 in 100 who kept esketamine. The company behind it paid for the trials, and critics argue some relapses may be effects of stopping, which the trial couldn't tell apart.

lines.short: Nobody has shown either way whether meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells.
lines.but: Scans show changes, but those can happen without nerve cells dying. Experts disagree.
how: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein, but it can drop without nerve cells dying.
Other markers of dopamine nerve endings are not always lower.
In two small studies the protein rose again after people stopped. Other studies found no link with time off meth.
On the other side, two health-record studies found Parkinson's more often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses (in one, about 3 vs 1 in 1,000 over 7 years). Some may be other conditions.

card.statement: Brain scans prove that meth kills dopamine nerve cells.
card.why: Scans show less of one dopamine protein in people who used heavily, but it can drop without nerve cells dying, and other markers aren't always lower. Experts disagree, and nobody has shown it either way.

items.what: 'the most common' is not in the lines

lines.short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.
lines.but: No doctor checked these answers and people chose to take part, so it can't show how common lasting numbness is after nitrous oxide.
how: A review pooled doctors' reports on 100 people with health problems after nitrous oxide (laughing gas): 57 had used it for fun, 25 in surgery.
80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Of 75 who had a spine scan, 51 showed a change in the spinal cord.
58 of 82 tested had low vitamin B12. But the search only found reports mentioning B12, so this is partly built in.
In an online survey, 200 of 4,633 people who used nitrous oxide in the past year reported numbness or tingling lasting days or weeks.

card.statement: In doctors' reports of harm from laughing gas, numbness or tingling was the most common problem.
card.why: Of 100 people in published reports, 80 had numbness or tingling and 58 had trouble walking. Not all used it for fun: 25 had been given it in surgery.

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

card.statement: Portugal's drug arrests fell mostly because having drugs for your own use stopped being a crime.
card.why: It became an offence handled by regional panels instead, so those cases left the crime count: crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to between 5,000 and 5,500 a year.

items.what: 'trained' staff is not in the lines

lines.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
lines.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In British Columbia in 2019, people took strips from ten harm-reduction sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.

card.statement: With opioids, take-home fentanyl strips showed fentanyl about as often as tests by trained staff.
card.why: In British Columbia, 90 in 100 take-home results on opioids showed fentanyl, against 89 in 100 on site; with meth and cocaine, home strips showed it far more often. The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.

lines.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
lines.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In British Columbia in 2019, people took strips from ten harm-reduction sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.

lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.

card.statement: In MDMA trials for PTSD, many people given a dummy pill plus therapy also no longer had PTSD.
card.why: 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill no longer had PTSD about 4 months later, against 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA. In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

lines.short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams.
lines.but: This comes second-hand from a review that did not check how good the studies were.
how: Studies asked people how they slept after stopping regular cannabis, and some recorded their sleep in a lab.
Between about a third and three quarters of those with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks.
In the lab they took longer to fall asleep and woke up more than before they stopped.
Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis.

card.statement: Stopping regular cannabis use can mess with your sleep and bring strange dreams.
card.why: Between about a third and three quarters of people with withdrawal symptoms had sleep problems, often with strange dreams for days or weeks, and in the lab they took longer to fall asleep. That's second-hand, from a review that didn't check how good the studies were.

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

card.statement: Caffeine makes people who rarely have it more alert.
card.why: In one lab study, caffeine made them faster but raised their jitters, not their alertness. It's one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits.

lines.short: Alcohol was listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.
lines.but: Alcohol is often left off death records, and these counts do not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008.
Alcohol was listed more often in men's deaths (17 in 100) than in women's (about 10 in 100).
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged alcohol involved in about 12 in 100 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Without knowing how many people drink with opioids, these counts cannot say how much alcohol adds to risk. Two reviews describe no study in people that measured it.

card.why: Death certificates have listed alcohol in about 15 of 100 opioid overdose deaths, a share steady since 2008, and more often for men than women. Alcohol is often left off death records, and counts like these can't say how much it adds to risk.

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.
lines.but: Small studies that only looked at blood cells under a microscope; the best had no group without LSD.
how: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells from two people in a lab dish, plus one patient with no 'before' test.
Two 1967 studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD, with no 'before' test. In one, patients on other drugs but no LSD had about as many breaks.
The best study tested 32 patients before and after pure LSD. Damaged cells went from about 4 in 100 to 6, maybe by chance.
All these studies looked at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs. A 1971 review linked raised breaks mainly to street LSD and many other drugs.

card.statement: The LSD chromosome scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish.
card.why: The cells came from just two people, plus a patient with no 'before' test; studies up to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. But those were small and looked only at blood cells under a microscope, not sperm or eggs.

lines.short: Sometimes. At one festival, 67 in 100 people handed over drugs that were not as sold.
lines.but: That was one festival, where chemists tested the drugs. After a strip showed fentanyl, few did.
how: At an English festival in 2016, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not as sold handed drugs over to be destroyed.
When the drug matched, 15 of 164 did. Staff saw these handovers, but people may have kept other drugs.
At a supervised injection site, people said they would throw the drug away after 11 in 100 checks that showed fentanyl, and after 7 in 100 that did not.
A review of drug checking services printed rates of 0 to 10 in 100 from four studies.

card.statement: When testing at one festival showed a drug wasn't as sold, most people handed drugs over to be destroyed.
card.why: At an English festival, 30 of 45 people whose drug wasn't as sold handed drugs over, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched. That was one festival with chemists doing the testing, and people may have kept other drugs.

lines.short: Barely. A single pill of Adderall (amphetamine) or methylphenidate gave healthy adults at most a small lift on some lab tests. In one trial, people felt helped; scores didn't rise.
lines.but: These studies tested a single pill in a lab, in healthy volunteers. Daily use, studying and exams were not tested.
how: In a US trial, 46 healthy young adults took Adderall or a dummy pill on different test days. None of 13 tests improved.
They still rated the Adderall pill as more helpful than the dummy pill, but feeling helped was not clearly linked to scoring better.
Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response.
A bigger boost to memory tested hours or days later came mostly from one lab's studies of men. Adjusted for missing studies, it nearly halved.

card.statement: Pills like Adderall give healthy people a big boost on thinking tests.
card.why: Across 48 studies of a single pill of amphetamine or methylphenidate, the average lift was small, clearest for holding back an automatic response. Daily use, studying and exams weren't tested.

lines.short: About 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017 also involved benzos.
lines.but: Death records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths does not measure risk.
how: US death certificates listed benzos in 21 of 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 9 in 1999.
Benzos were listed more often with prescription opioids or methadone (about 1 in 3) than with heroin or fentanyl.
In North Carolina in 2010, medical examiners, who investigate deaths, judged benzos involved in about 6 in 10 deaths involving an opioid painkiller.
Of people on prescribed opioids who died of overdose, half (US veterans) to three in four (Ontario) had benzo prescriptions.

card.statement: Benzos were listed in about 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017.
card.why: That's 21 in 100 death certificates, up from 9 in 1999, with benzos listed more often alongside prescription opioids or methadone than heroin or fentanyl. Records miss some drugs, and a share of deaths doesn't measure risk.

In 2008, US heart doctors advised against beta-blockers for chest pain after cocaine. That rests mainly on small lab tests, animal tests and expert opinion.

lines.short: Some deaths are missing; others are counted without showing which drug was involved.
lines.but: The gaps differ by place and rules. Most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.
how: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 out of 100 overdoses had only an unspecified-drug code.
Models guessed which drugs those counted deaths involved. They did not find deaths missing from the total.
In Stockholm, lists with similar totals disagreed about which people to include. They used different rules.
An England and Wales estimate suggests counts held about two thirds of deaths involving each opioid. It did not match each death across lists.

card.statement: Official records name the drug involved in nearly every overdose death.
card.why: In US records from 1999 to 2015, about 23 in 100 overdose deaths had only an 'unspecified drug' code. The gaps differ by place and rules, and most evidence concerns older US opioid deaths.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. People who had stopped did as well as people who don't use it.
lines.but: The people who had stopped had mostly used less, and nobody was tested before starting.
how: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well on memory tests as people who don't use ketamine. They still did a year later.
But most of them had used less than the people who used most days, so this does not show that stopping fixed anything.
In 18 people who had cut down, one word test caught up after 3 to 4 years. Story memory and speed stayed lower, as at their first test.
People who were still using also scored better on average a year later, perhaps partly from practice.

card.statement: People who've quit ketamine do worse on memory tests than people who don't use it.
card.why: In one London team's study, 30 people who had stopped for at least a month did as well as people who don't use ketamine, and still did a year later. But most had used less than people who used most days, so this doesn't show stopping fixed anything.

lines.short: People dependent on meth reported more crime in months when they used it.
lines.but: One study, and it could not show which came first.
how: In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth were followed for up to three years. Each person's months with meth were compared with their own months without.
Some crime was reported in 56 of 100 months with meth use and about 18 of 100 without.
The link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime. It stayed after other drug use and money and housing problems were counted.
People reported use and crime for the same months, and treatment or time in prison was not counted.

card.statement: In one study, violent crime was the crime most tied to months of meth use.
card.why: Among 469 people dependent on meth in Australia, the link was strongest for selling drugs and property crime, even after money and housing problems were counted. People reported use and crime for the same months, so it can't show which came first.

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

card.statement: Two months on, most volunteers in one lab study ranked their psilocybin session among their five most meaningful experiences.
card.why: About 2 in 3 put it in their top five, and most who answered said it had raised their wellbeing. But everyone in the study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have shaped how they saw it.

lines.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
lines.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.

card.statement: Teen cannabis use went up after US states made recreational cannabis legal.
card.why: Not in one big study of 1.4 million US high school answers: after recreational laws, teens were a bit less likely to say they'd used it in the past month. But only 7 states had surveys from before and after, and only for the first few years.

lines.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
lines.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, which had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.

card.statement: Eating poppy seeds can make you fail a sports drug test.
card.why: In a German study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake went over the sports limit of the time for morphine in their urine. But the cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested, and workplace tests weren't studied.

lines.short: It may. In one trial, 42 in 100 given psilocybin kept their depression score at least halved from week 1 to week 6, against 11 in 100 given a vitamin pill.
lines.but: People could probably tell they had taken psilocybin, and nobody checked, which may have made the gap look bigger.
how: In 10 countries, 233 adults whose depression had resisted 2 to 4 treatments got a full, medium or tiny psilocybin dose.
After 3 weeks, only the full psilocybin dose showed bigger falls in depression than the tiny dose. By 12 weeks the gap could be chance.
In the US, 104 adults got psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin that makes skin flush. Depression scores fell more with psilocybin, through 6 weeks.
In the bigger trial, serious suicidal thoughts or self-harm happened on every dose, more often on higher ones. The US trial recorded none.

card.statement: In a big trial for hard-to-treat depression, psilocybin's benefit was still clear at 12 weeks.
card.why: In 233 adults across 10 countries, only the full dose beat a tiny one at 3 weeks, and by 12 weeks the gap could be chance.

how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

card.statement: Most US soldiers who were hooked on narcotics in Vietnam stayed hooked after coming home.
card.why: About 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics in Vietnam, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.

lines.short: More side effects than with a dummy, such as dizziness, feeling high, confusion and dry mouth.

card.why: In trials, about 81 in 100 people on cannabis medicines had at least one, such as dizziness or dry mouth, against 62 in 100 on a dummy or another medicine, and more quit because of them. The trials were short, and long-term harms weren't studied.

lines.short: Ecstasy pills are often MDMA, but not always, and the amount varies a lot.
lines.but: These tests end around 2002, so they may not describe pills today.
how: A 2004 review of pill tests estimated that 90 to 98 in 100 ecstasy pills held MDMA from the 1980s to the early 1990s, 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. The rest held related drugs, other things such as ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active.
The amount of MDMA in a pill ranged from none to several times more than in others, and some pills held a different drug.
People in an Australian survey thought about 1 pill in 4 or 5 was a dud.

Some people feel little from a pill, and some then take more. A weaker pill, or one with no MDMA, is one possible reason. The review did not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, or at what happens when people then take more.

card.statement: Ecstasy pills always contain MDMA.
card.why: A 2004 review of pill tests estimated that only 50 to 80 in 100 held MDMA in the mid-1990s, though nearly all did by the early 2000s; others held related drugs, things like ketamine or caffeine, or nothing active. The tests end around 2002, so pills today may differ.

lines.short: It has not been shown that ecstasy harms dopamine nerve cells in people.
lines.but: Very little has been measured in people, so this does not show it is safe.
how: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn: the animals got a different drug.
A review found five human scan studies, and none showed a clear dopamine change.
In one, the dopamine marker was lower only in people who had also used amphetamine recently.
A by-product in spinal fluid cannot show whether nerve cells were harmed.

card.statement: Ecstasy has been shown to damage dopamine nerve cells in people.
card.why: The study that claimed this harm was withdrawn because its animals got a different drug, and five human scan studies showed no clear dopamine change. But very little has been measured in people, so this doesn't show it's safe.

lines.short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.
lines.but: These are computer estimates built on studies of groups of people, not counted deaths.
how: The Global Burden of Disease study estimated 2.8 million deaths in 2016: about 7 in 100 deaths of men and 2 in 100 of women.
At ages 15 to 49, alcohol was the top risk factor in that study: about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women.
An older model using WHO data estimated about 2.5 million deaths caused in 2004, mostly from injuries, heart disease, cancer and cirrhosis, minus about 0.2 million it counted as prevented.
A later round of the global study, quoted second-hand, put it at about 1.8 million in 2020. The numbers move with the method, so they do not show a trend.

card.statement: In a global study, alcohol was the top risk factor for death among people aged 15 to 49.
card.why: The Global Burden of Disease study put about 12 in 100 deaths of men and 4 in 100 of women at those ages down to alcohol. These are computer estimates, not counted deaths.

lines.short: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.
lines.but: This comes from questionnaires, retold in one review; no laboratory study has tested it.
how: In surveys, most people say the first time was the strongest.
People who have used more say they take more tablets in a night.
Nobody checked what the tablets held, and different people were compared, not followed over time.
In one study, longer use did not go with more tablets.

card.why: In questionnaires retold in one review, most said the first time was the strongest. But nobody checked what the tablets held, different people were compared rather than followed, and no lab study has tested it.

how: People dependent on meth stopped using on a hospital research ward.
Most symptoms they reported eased within one to two weeks.
Low mood lasted about three weeks; craving lasted to week five, at a lower level.
They were not looking for treatment. None had another mental-health diagnosis at the time.

card.statement: Meth cravings go away as quickly as the other withdrawal symptoms.
card.why: In one small hospital-ward study, most symptoms eased within one to two weeks and low mood lasted about three, but craving lasted to week five, though weaker. The people in it weren't seeking treatment.

lines.short: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover.
lines.but: These are memories from a 2011 online survey; nobody tested the products.
how: About a thousand people who had used both compared them in an online survey.
They said synthetic cannabis made it harder to get on with things afterwards.
They said it gave more bad feelings and fear of others while high, and much less enjoyment.
Most preferred ordinary cannabis, and said synthetic cannabis wore off sooner.

card.statement: People who've used both say synthetic cannabis is as enjoyable as ordinary cannabis.
card.why: In a 2011 online survey of about a thousand people who'd used both, they reported much less enjoyment, more bad feelings and more fear of others, and most preferred ordinary cannabis. Nobody tested the products.

how: Acamprosate is a tablet. Most trials were in Europe, in people who had already stopped drinking.
About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again during treatment, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills. It did not cut heavy drinking.

card.why: About 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 in 100 on dummy pills, and the most carefully run trials found no clear difference. Most trials were run or supported by drug companies, mostly its maker.

card.statement: Caffeine can set off panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
card.why: In 10 small lab studies, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder had a panic attack after caffeine, and none were reported after a dummy. What ordinary, smaller servings do isn't known.

lines.short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.
lines.but: Shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain the cannabis link.
how: In New Zealand, at least 86 in 100 young people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis a year or more before.
Australian twins grew up together. The one starting cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants: 48 in 100 against 26 in 100.
A computer model where cannabis did nothing still made the same pattern. Some people were likelier to use any drug, and were offered cannabis first.
Experts disagreed about the New Zealand cannabis link. One said hidden factors no longer explain it away; another said factors changing with age still could.

card.statement: In one twin study, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used cocaine or other stimulants.
card.why: It was 48 in 100 against 26 in 100, in Australian twins who grew up together. That's a link, not proof cannabis led on: shared risks and access to other drugs could still explain it.

lines.short: With ketamine for depression, studies most often found headache and dizziness. Next came feeling unreal and higher blood pressure. Most soon passed.
lines.but: Only 12 of 60 studies checked again 2 weeks or more after the last dose, and just 5 checked the bladder.
how: A review of 60 studies up to 2016 listed side effects but could not say how often each happens. Most people had a single dose.
Raised blood pressure and heart rate came during or just after the drip and mostly settled within 90 minutes.
In a 7-person trial, all felt 'high' on ketamine and none on salt water. On average it was gone within 2 hours after the drip.
In a large trial, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect within 3 weeks, against 32 in 100 on ECT.

card.statement: In a big trial, ketamine treatment for depression caused more moderate or severe side effects than ECT.
card.why: Within 3 weeks, 25 in 100 on ketamine had a moderate or severe side effect, against 32 in 100 on ECT. Across studies, headache and dizziness were most common, and most side effects soon passed.

lines.short: In a typical study of people with meth psychosis, about 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
lines.but: Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.
how: A review of 27 studies, mostly of hospital patients, looked at how long symptoms lasted.
In the typical study, 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.
How many were later told they had schizophrenia varied a lot between studies, from about 1 in 20 to 2 in 5. One review's average was about 1 in 5. This does not show that meth caused it.
Psychosis often comes back when people use again.

card.statement: Psychosis linked to meth always clears up within a month of stopping.
card.why: In a typical study, about 1 in 4 people with meth psychosis still had symptoms over a month after stopping. Studies ranged from none to almost all, and most were of hospital patients.

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

card.statement: A meth overdose shows up as slow breathing and tiny pupils.
card.why: It's the reverse: it looks like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils and great restlessness. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

lines.short: Maybe a little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled a bit less fear. They also reported fewer problems later.
lines.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear. Church hymns or sermons went with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.

card.statement: The more traditional the ayahuasca ceremony, the less fear people feel.
card.why: In one big survey, more traditional practices went with a little more fear, and church hymns or sermons with less. The differences were small, and people rated everything looking back.

lines.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.

card.statement: Lots of people who take magic mushrooms end up seeking emergency treatment.
card.why: In one big online survey, about 2 in 1,000 people who'd used them in the past year said they had, and nearly all of those felt back to normal within a day. But nobody checked their answers, and anyone who couldn't answer wasn't counted.

lines.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
lines.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it harder to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after ketamine. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.

card.statement: One ketamine drip can lift depression within hours.
card.why: A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. But for most the lift faded within weeks, and people can often tell they got ketamine, which may make it look bigger.

lines.short: No sign they did. Despite nearly $1 billion from Congress, teens' reported cannabis use stayed flat in a national survey, and those who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.
lines.but: Nearly every teen saw the ads, so there was no group without them to compare cannabis use with.
how: A national survey interviewed 8,117 US kids aged 9 to 18 at home, and many again up to three times, between 1999 and 2004.
94 in 100 remembered seeing anti-drug ads at least monthly. About 24 in 100 teens said they'd ever used cannabis, in 2000 and again in 2004.
Teens who remembered more ads were no less likely to start cannabis by the next interview. Fewer said they definitely wouldn't.
In one of three periods, more ads even went with more first use of cannabis. The authors call this tentative, not definitive.

card.statement: Teens who remembered more of the US government's anti-drug ads were, if anything, more likely to try cannabis.
card.why: In a national survey, they were no less likely to start, fewer said they definitely wouldn't, and in one of three periods more ads went with more first use. The authors call that tentative, not definitive.

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

card.statement: Almost everyone who tries stimulants like meth gets hooked.
card.why: It depends how you count: an old US survey found about 11 in 100 had ever been dependent, and a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years. Neither had a number for meth alone.

lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, so drinking more than it needs waters down the salt. The UK authors say how it happens is not yet known.

card.statement: In UK reports, most people with low blood salt after MDMA had drunk a lot of liquid.
card.why: At least 10 of 17 cases reported to a UK poisons service had, and the 2 who died had brain swelling. These reports count only people who got ill, so they can't show how often it happens or whether drinking more changes the risk.

lines.short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.
lines.but: Most samples were cannabis seized by police, not picked at random, so they may not match what people buy.
how: Researchers combined 12 studies from 7 countries that measured THC in cannabis. Most tested police seizures; two Dutch studies bought samples at random in shops.
A point is a share of the weight: 5% to 6% THC is one point. These numbers describe the cannabis, not what people took in.
Not everywhere: US weed rose in every period studied, but weed in the UK (1975–1989) and New Zealand (1979–1996) showed no clear rise.
CBD, another substance in cannabis, did not change. The authors put the weed rise down to stronger kinds selling more, but sales were not measured.

card.statement: Weed really is stronger than it used to be, on average.
card.why: Across 7 countries from 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash. But most samples were seized by police, so they may not match what people buy.

lines.short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.
lines.but: People were tested only after they had started, so the studies can't show that cannabis caused it.
how: A review pooled 69 studies of young people, about 21 years old on average, who used cannabis often.
They scored a little lower on learning, memory, attention and planning tests. Language, shape and movement tests showed no clear gap.
The gap was smaller in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days before the test, and bigger in people getting help for their cannabis use. Small studies found bigger gaps.
In a British twin study, the gap at age 18 was no longer clear when each twin was compared with their own twin.

card.statement: On average, people who often use cannabis score a little lower on memory tests.
card.why: A big review found small gaps in learning, memory, attention and planning, but none clear for language, shape or movement. People were tested only after they'd started, so it can't show cannabis caused the gap.

lines.short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.
lines.but: Fewer newspapers told readers about the mistake than told the first story.
how: The animals had been given a different drug, from a wrongly labelled bottle.
Two of the ten animals given the drug died during the study.
Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.
The notice does not say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

card.statement: The 2002 study claiming ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains had actually given the animals a different drug.
card.why: The drug came from a wrongly labelled bottle, and the study was withdrawn a year later. The withdrawal notice doesn't say what the one animal that got ecstasy showed.

lines.short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.
lines.but: One Swedish study. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.
how: In Sweden, 18,115 adopted children born 1950 to 1993 were followed in health, prescription and court records until 2009.
Some birth parents had a drug problem on record. Their children, raised by adoptive parents, had one about twice as often: about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did.
Adoptive brothers and sisters are not related by birth. Still, 6 in 100 of them had a drug problem when the adopted child had one, against 3 in 100 when the child did not.

The study did not work out a share due to genes. Where studies give one, it is about differences between people in one place and time. It does not say how much of your own risk comes from genes, and it can change when living conditions change.

card.statement: Children adopted away from a birth parent with a drug problem still have drug problems more often.
card.why: In a Swedish study, about 9 in 100 of them had one on record, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did. What birth parents pass on includes the pregnancy, not just genes.

lines.short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.
lines.but: The cases were selected for reports. They cannot give the risk per encounter.
how: The reviews describe extreme agitation, but no validated definition or specific autopsy sign. The label is also used with living people.
In 168 published cases, force was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths. That included sedation and electrical weapons as well as physical restraint.
Only 3 cases explicitly had no force; 28 had missing information. A later review also cites deaths attributed to the label without overt restraint.
Researchers disagree about restraint, drugs and the agitated state. These reports cannot tell how much each caused.

card.statement: In most published 'excited delirium' deaths, force such as restraint was recorded.
card.why: Force, including sedation and electrical weapons as well as restraint, was recorded in 94 of 104 deaths among published cases. These were selected reports, so they can't tell how much restraint, drugs or the agitated state caused a death.

lines.short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.
lines.but: Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.
how: Alcohol use disorder is found with a list of 11 signs of problem drinking: 2 or more in a year count. In 2012 and 2013, a US survey asked 36,309 adults set questions to find it.
About 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year, and 29 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild. It was most common at ages 18 to 29: about 27 in 100.
The survey's authors think it became more common after 2001. We think their two surveys were run too differently to show that.
The survey missed people who were homeless or in prison, and most people in treatment. For the world, a review passes on an estimate of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older.

card.statement: In one US survey, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year.
card.why: Two or more of 11 signs of problem drinking in a year count, and about half the cases were mild. Another US survey found a little over half as many, so the number depends on the survey.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

card.statement: Caffeine doesn't really change how much you sleep that night.
card.why: Across 24 studies comparing nights with and without caffeine in the same people, they slept about 45 minutes less after caffeine, and their sleep was lighter. These were healthy adults with low to moderate usual intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.

lines.short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.
lines.but: Only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined three trials. People having chemotherapy got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
About 47 in 100 people on the medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on the dummy.
Most other trials compared cannabis medicines with other sickness medicines. The review says these leaned towards cannabis too. But it did not combine them.
23 of the 28 trials had serious weaknesses in how they were run or reported.

card.statement: In small trials, cannabis medicines controlled sickness from chemotherapy better than a dummy did.
card.why: About 47 in 100 on a cannabis medicine had their sickness fully controlled, against 20 in 100 on a dummy. But only 102 people were in these three trials, and most trials in the review had serious weaknesses.

lines.short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.
lines.but: It looked at laws, not at people using strips. Other changes at the same time could explain it.
how: Researchers used death records from every US state from 2018 to 2022. They counted 15 states and Washington, DC as making the strips legal in that time.

After the law, there were about 3 fewer drug deaths a year for every 100,000 people, about 7 in 100 fewer than expected. Once age, rural living and income were allowed for, this was about the same for White and Black people, though less certain for Black people.
The study did not check whether more people got or used strips. It counted deaths from any drug, and the drop came in the very first month of each law.

The researchers chose the law dates themselves. They kept Alabama, Minnesota and New Mexico among the states without a law, though laws started there in 2021 and 2022, and moved two other dates later. They showed no results with their source's dates.

card.statement: Making fentanyl test strips legal has been shown to cut drug deaths.
card.why: After the laws, deaths ran about 7 in 100 below the expected trend, but the study didn't check whether more people used strips, and the drop came in each law's very first month. Other changes at the same time could explain it.

lines.short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs.
lines.but: That one Dutch study cannot show GHB caused the memory problems, and nobody checked if they improve.
how: Lab studies found that GHB affects memory and coordination while it is working.
The review says it is not yet known whether these short-term memory effects fully wear off.
One study found that people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs but never GHB.

card.statement: Passing out from GHB again and again has been linked to worse memory.
card.why: In one Dutch study, people who had passed out many times remembered worse than people who used GHB regularly without passing out, and than people who used other drugs. It can't show GHB caused it, and nobody checked whether memory improves.

lines.short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.
lines.but: Everyone knew whether they got ketamine or ECT, and the trials took different people, so nobody knows why they disagree.
how: In a US trial of 403 adults, mostly outpatients without psychosis, 55 in 100 on ketamine drips said their depression halved, against 41 on ECT.
In a Swedish trial of 186 hospital patients, some with psychosis, 63 in 100 got well after ECT, against 46 after ketamine.
A review combining hospital trials also found ECT eased depression more than ketamine, but about half its data came from that Swedish trial.
In Sweden, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips.

card.statement: Ketamine drips for depression cause memory loss as often as ECT does.
card.why: In a Swedish trial, 19 of 90 had memory loss lasting over a day after ECT, against none of 91 after ketamine drips. Everyone knew which treatment they got.
