lines.short: In people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drug, memory scores were no different.
lines.but: It was one study, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out.
how: 52 people who used ecstasy were compared with 59 people from the same all-night dance scene.
Breath, urine and hair tests checked that they had used little else.
Memory scores did not differ, and most of the 40 measures were similar.
People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test.

card.statement: People who use ecstasy score worse on memory tests even if they use hardly any other drug.
card.why: In one study where breath, urine and hair tests checked that people used little else, memory scores didn't differ from others in the same all-night dance scene. Medium-sized differences couldn't be ruled out, and heavier use went with worse scores on one planning test.

lines.short: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis.
lines.but: It stays rare: about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years. Some diagnoses are probably other conditions, and medicine side effects were not ruled out.
how: In Utah health records, Parkinson's was diagnosed about 3 times as often in people with meth or amphetamine diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnoses.
That is about 3 in 1,000 against 1 in 1,000, over about 7 years.
A California study found a smaller increase.
The records probably include other movement conditions.

card.statement: Parkinson's disease is common in people diagnosed with meth or amphetamine problems.
card.why: In Utah health records of people with such diagnoses and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis, it was diagnosed about 3 times as often, but that's about 3 in 1,000 over about 7 years, against 1 in 1,000. Some diagnoses were probably other movement conditions.

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

card.statement: In most recent US overdose deaths involving meth, meth was the only drug.
card.why: Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024 found fentanyl or other opioids in about 7 in 10 of these deaths. That's a different kind of record from the yearly death counts.

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.

card.statement: The link between cannabis and car crashes stays just as strong when studies allow for drinking.
card.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.

lines.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
lines.but: The reviews give no numbers. Not how long a break must be, or how much the risk of a fatal overdose rises.
how: The older review offers this as a possible explanation. It says tolerance may fade quickly, and not at the same pace for every effect. But there's little data on how fast.
The idea rests on one hair study. People who died of heroin overdose had less morphine in their hair than people still using. The review reads that as less use before death.
The newer review gives prison and detox as examples of a break; the older one, which it cites, doesn't.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.

card.statement: People on methadone become fully tolerant to its effect on breathing.
card.why: In two studies of people on methadone, tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete. Reviews add that tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, so the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
lines.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.

card.statement: Music has been shown to make ketamine treatment for depression work better.
card.why: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how well ketamine works. In a trial of 32 patients, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music, and the report gave no results on how sessions felt.

lines.short: Fairly common: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip. 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life.
lines.but: That's one online survey, and people were looking back over their whole lives.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

card.statement: Bad trips are fairly common among people who've used psychedelics.
card.why: 41 in 100 people who'd used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip, and 5 in 100 said one had badly affected their daily life. That's one online survey of US adults looking back over their whole lives.

lines.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.

card.statement: Psilocybin has been shown to help people quit smoking.
card.why: In one small study, 12 of just 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later. With no comparison group, no one can tell what psilocybin added.

lines.short: It depends how you count. An old US survey found 11 in 100 had ever been dependent; a broader Australian count estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting.
lines.but: Neither survey has a number for meth alone, and the two measured different things, so they can't be compared directly.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey in 2007 counted differently, allowing for when people started. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years of starting, but it also counted a related diagnosis called abuse.

card.statement: A US survey found tobacco hooked a bigger share of people who'd used it than cocaine or meth-like stimulants.
card.why: Tobacco 32 in 100, cocaine 17, stimulants other than cocaine about 11, in an early-1990s survey that included people who'd only just started. A broader Australian count, done differently, estimated about 50 in 100 for stimulants within 14 years of starting.

lines.short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.
lines.but: Strength was guessed from the type people named, and both studies come from one team.
how: Two studies by one team, one in south London and one in 11 places in Europe and Brazil, compared people who had a first psychosis with people from the same areas who had not.

In 11 places in Europe and Brazil, daily use of strong types (10% THC or more on average) went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis, compared with never using. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times; the gap between the two could be chance.

In the 11 places, using any type only now and then was not linked to psychosis. In London, using strong types less than once a week went with nearly 2 times the odds, but some numbers in that study do not add up. In both studies, weaker types were not linked once all patterns of use were counted together.
Nobody tested the cannabis: people named the type they had used after they became ill, and its strength was taken from police, European and national figures.

card.statement: In one study, daily use of strong cannabis went with about 5 times the odds of psychosis.
card.why: That's compared with never using, in 11 places in Europe and Brazil. Daily use of weaker types went with about 2 times, and the gap between strong and weaker could be chance.

items.what: pooled figures said as if each study found them

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
lines.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.

card.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
card.why: A review of three studies each found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.
lines.but: Only three studies each, mostly measured in the teen years; they cannot show cause.
how: A review combined three long-term studies on suicidal thoughts and three on suicide attempts.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and about 3.5 times the odds of attempts, compared with teens who did not use cannabis.
In two of the three studies for each, this was measured while the young people were still teenagers.
In other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were taken into account.

card.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than teens who don't.
card.why: Combining three studies on thoughts and three on attempts, a review found about 1.5 times the odds of suicidal thoughts and 3.5 times the odds of attempts in teens who used the most. That can't show cause: in other studies, the link shrank or went away once depression, alcohol and hard living conditions were counted.

lines.short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.
lines.but: The checklist was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses, against that unit's own diagnosis.
how: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) is too much serotonin activity, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. It ranges from mild to severe.
Doctors examine the person for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever.
In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs matched the unit's diagnosis in about 84 of 100 people diagnosed. An older checklist matched about 75 of 100.
Everyone had taken an overdose, and mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects. No independent test of the checklist was found.

card.statement: Mild serotonin syndrome is easy to tell apart from ordinary drug effects.
card.why: Mild signs can look like ordinary drug effects; doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking with very brisk reflexes, sweating and restlessness, and, when severe, stiff muscles with a high fever. A checklist of these signs was tested in one hospital unit, on overdoses.

lines.short: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made people drive worse the next day than after dummy pills.
lines.but: Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.
how: Volunteers drove a real car or a driving machine the day after a pill or a dummy pill.
Researchers measured how much the car weaved inside its lane.
With some pills the weaving was worse than with alcohol at the driving limit used in several countries.
With other pills or lower doses, weaving was not clearly different from dummy pills, but each result came from one small study.

card.statement: The day after some benzo sleeping pills, people drove worse than with alcohol at a common drink-driving limit.
card.why: In tests in a real car or a driving machine, weaving inside the lane was worse with some pills than with alcohol at the limit used in several countries. Most studies tested one night in healthy volunteers, not people who take these pills for months.

lines.short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.
lines.but: Only 7 people had no working enzyme, and no study gave a second dose of MDMA.
how: Among 139 volunteers in eight lab studies, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 had a peak MDMA level about 15 percent higher, in the first 3 hours only.
In 15 men, tests after one MDMA dose looked like those of people with no working enzyme in 10 of them. The enzyme had not fully recovered after 10 days.
Medicines that block the enzyme raised the MDMA peak by about 15 to 20 percent. Paroxetine raised it by 16 percent in 12 men.
Bodies that differ are one reason a person can feel little from an amount and take more. None of these studies gave a second dose, so what happens then is not known.

card.statement: People with no working version of the enzyme that clears MDMA get far higher levels of it.
card.why: Their peak level was only about 15 percent higher, and only in the first 3 hours: MDMA seems to switch that enzyme off itself, so these body differences matter less. Just 7 such people were studied.

lines.short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.
lines.but: All of this was in rats, so it says nothing direct about people.
how: In 1979, by the last test, rats kept alone drank 5 to over 16 times as much sweet morphine water as rats living together.
In 1978, when morphine water was almost all they had to drink, the rats living together drank more of it.
In all three studies, the two groups drank morphine water from different machines, measured differently. That could explain part of the gap.
Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result.

card.statement: Rat Park has been repeated, with the same result.
card.why: Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 Rat Park morphine study did not find the same result. In the original studies, the two groups also drank from different machines, measured differently, and all of it was in rats.

lines.short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.
lines.but: Each brain was scanned once, so the study shows a link, not shrinking, and not that alcohol caused it.
how: 527 UK government workers, mostly men, reported how much alcohol they drank over 30 years, then had one brain scan around age 70.
'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. Even 35 in 100 people who barely drank alcohol got that rating.
The paper's 'three times the odds' came from the top of its 'moderate' range for men; lower down, the study was too small to tell.
Only one of three thinking tests (naming words that start with a letter) fell slightly faster with more drinking. No test at the scan differed.

card.statement: In a UK scan study, 35 in 100 people who barely drank had a memory area rated 'shrunken'.
card.why: 'Shrunken' meant doctors saw any sign of shrinkage at all. People who drank more got the rating more often, but the study can't show alcohol caused it.

lines.short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.
lines.but: Most figures are passed on by one review or come from old trials, mostly one from 1969.
how: The DTs are confusion that comes on fast and comes and goes, together with signs of withdrawal such as shaking or a fast pulse.
A review says the DTs usually start about 3 days after withdrawal begins and last 2 or 3 days. It says 3 to 5 in 100 people in hospital for withdrawal get them.
In old trials, about 6 in 100 people in withdrawal who got dummy pills developed delirium. Most of these people were in one trial from 1969.
The review says about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. It names recent seizures, earlier DTs, older age and other illnesses as signs they are more likely.

card.statement: Most people treated in hospital for alcohol withdrawal get the DTs (sudden confusion).
card.why: A review says 3 to 5 in 100 of them do, and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with the DTs die. Most of these figures are passed on by that review or come from old trials.

lines.short: 68 in 100 people treated for cocaine reported psychotic symptoms; 16 in 100 had a diagnosed disorder.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, and many also used alcohol or other drugs.
how: One review pooled 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine in the US and Spain.
Asked about symptoms such as paranoia, 68 in 100 said they had had them with cocaine. Strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100.
The review could not separate cocaine from the alcohol and other drugs people used, so it cannot show cocaine alone caused it.
Other studies the review cites say the symptoms usually pass after stopping, but can get worse with more use and last for weeks.

card.statement: Most people in treatment for cocaine say they've had paranoia or similar symptoms with it.
card.why: In a review of 17 studies, 68 in 100 said so, while strict diagnostic interviews found a psychotic disorder in 16 in 100. Many also used alcohol or other drugs, so the review can't show cocaine alone caused it.

lines.short: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy in pregnancy, but it cannot show cause.
lines.but: There was no comparison group, and almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up.
how: A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used, nearly all in the first 3 months. 62 of them also involved other drugs.
Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones. The authors expected 2 to 3 in 100.
Two babies had heart defects and three had a twisted foot. The authors say the study is too small to confirm a link with any one defect.

A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects. One baby had a rare genetic condition, which the authors say cannot be tied to the mother's drug use.

card.statement: In one study, more babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy had birth defects than expected.
card.why: 12 of 78 babies born alive, about 15 in 100, had a birth defect, against the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and many pregnancies also involved other drugs.

lines.short: In three trials, people on a depression medicine, mirtazapine, used somewhat less meth than on a dummy pill.
lines.but: Most people kept using, and in the largest trial drug tests showed no difference.
how: Two small San Francisco trials, in men who have sex with men who also had counselling, found fewer meth-positive urine tests on mirtazapine.
A larger Australian trial: people said they cut down by about 2 more days in 4 weeks.
Its saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most people kept using.
Drowsiness was more common on mirtazapine.

card.statement: In the largest trial, drug tests confirmed the antidepressant mirtazapine cut meth use.
card.why: People on mirtazapine said they used meth about 2 fewer days in 4 weeks than people on a dummy pill, but saliva drug tests showed no difference, and most kept using. Two small San Francisco trials did find fewer meth-positive urine tests.

lines.short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.
lines.but: Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids. The rise slowed after 2021.
how: In US surveys, past-year meth use rose by about a fifth from 2015 to 2019.
Deaths involving meth rose from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023. The rise slowed after 2021.
Medical examiners' reports from 2021 to mid-2024: about 7 in 10 overdose deaths involving meth also involved opioids. This is a different kind of record from the death counts.
The surveys miss people who are homeless or living in places like prisons and hospitals.

card.statement: US deaths involving meth were still rising in 2023.
card.why: They went from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, though the rise slowed after 2021. Many of these deaths also involved fentanyl or other opioids.

lines.short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.
lines.but: This comes from one expert's summary of older studies; it does not say how many people get each feeling.
how: The studies asked the same people how they felt before and after they stopped smoking.
Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks.
Feeling tired, headaches and sweating did not go up after stopping.
For some people the feelings lasted longer or came back after about three weeks.

card.statement: The grumpiness and restlessness of quitting smoking usually last for months.
card.why: Most of these feelings were strongest in the first week and gone within 2 to 4 weeks, though for some people they lasted longer or came back. That comes from one expert's summary of older studies.

lines.short: In three reported cases, a severe breakdown lasted two to four weeks, then passed.
lines.but: Only three cases from 1975, and nobody tested the drugs they had taken.
how: Three young men were treated in one hospital after street drugs thought to contain PCP.
They were confused, angry and unsteady, two heard voices, and one jumped from a high window.
All three got better, and afterwards remembered little of their illness.
Earlier studies the doctors cited said the mind effects of PCP usually last about a day.

card.statement: A bad reaction to PCP always wears off within about a day.
card.why: In three cases reported in 1975, a severe breakdown after drugs thought to contain PCP lasted two to four weeks, then passed. Only three cases, and nobody tested the drugs they'd taken.

lines.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
lines.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

card.statement: Few people who go to harm reduction sites use drugs alone.
card.why: In a survey at 27 sites in British Columbia, about 3 in 4 had used alone at least once in the past week, most often because it was easier and more comfortable at home. It's one survey, of people already going to these sites.

lines.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year, and answered, said they'd sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.

card.statement: In one big survey, people sought emergency treatment more often after LSD than after magic mushrooms.
card.why: About 10 in 1,000 people who'd used LSD in the past year said they had, mostly for panic, anxiety or confusion, against 2 in 1,000 after magic mushrooms. Nobody checked the answers, or whether the drug was really LSD.

lines.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
lines.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.

card.statement: In a UK study, readers judged a man who died from drugs more harshly than a woman.
card.why: With story details picked at random, readers were also harsher when the story said heroin rather than ecstasy, or an older person with years of use. The differences were small to moderate, and readers answered straight after one made-up story.

lines.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.

card.statement: MDMA only raises body temperature when people dance in hot, crowded places.
card.why: Even resting in a room at about 23 degrees, 24 in 100 lab volunteers went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill. Heat, dancing and crowds weren't tested.

lines.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
lines.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.

card.statement: People who had their first drink at 14 or younger more often had alcohol dependence than late starters.
card.why: In a big US survey, about 4 to 5 in 10 who started at 14 or younger had been dependent at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. But people had to remember their first drink, and some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

card.statement: The serotonin changes seen on scans of people who used ecstasy are known to be permanent.
card.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

lines.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
lines.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.

card.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with an MAOI antidepressant, like moclobemide, as the riskiest mix they list.
card.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

lines.short: After a binge, people described a crash: very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger.
lines.but: This is what some people in treatment told their doctors; it cannot show how often it happens.
how: Doctors talked with 30 people who came for help with heavy cocaine use; there was no comparison group.
The crash began soon after the last use and usually ended within a few days.
Some people had passing thoughts of suicide, which were limited to the crash.
Many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep.

card.statement: People describe the crash after a cocaine binge as very low mood, then long, heavy sleep.
card.why: Thirty people who sought help for heavy cocaine use also described hunger, and some had passing thoughts of suicide that stayed within the crash. It's what people in treatment told their doctors, so it can't show how often this happens.

items.what: a word the lines do not hold ('severe'); the answer turns on a technicality

lines.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
lines.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.

card.statement: In trials, a CBD medicine at least halved seizures for most children with Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy.
card.why: It did for 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up.

lines.short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.
lines.but: The maker ran both trials, and in its own backup checks the result did not always hold up.
how: First trial, 120 children: seizures at least halved in 43 in 100 on CBD and 27 on the dummy liquid. That gap could be chance.
Second trial, 198 children: 44 and 49 in 100 in two CBD groups saw seizures at least halve. On the dummy liquid, 26 did.
The second report said backup checks agreed. Yet with missing diary days filled in, one CBD group no longer clearly beat the dummy liquid.
On CBD, 23 to 36 in 100 children were sleepy, against 10 to 14 on the dummy liquid. Shop CBD was not tested.

card.statement: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in children with Dravet syndrome, a form of epilepsy.
card.why: Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children on it, against 26 to 27 in 100 on a dummy liquid. But the maker ran both trials, in its own backup checks the result didn't always hold up, and shop CBD wasn't tested.

items.what: gives a reason the lines do not give

lines.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
lines.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.

card.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
card.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep in the first week after stopping. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, so how long it lasts isn't known.

lines.short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.
lines.but: Three small studies, two of them from the 1970s with very strong lab doses.
how: Sleep was measured in a lab while people were still using cannabis and after they stopped.
After stopping, they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and had more dream (REM) sleep.
The pooled data came from the first week after stopping, so this review cannot say how long the changes last.

card.statement: In sleep labs, people who stopped heavy cannabis use got more dream sleep in the first nights.
card.why: They also slept less and took longer to fall asleep. That's from three small studies, two of them from the 1970s, and the data cover only the first week after stopping, so how long it lasts isn't known.

lines.short: In lab tests, strips found most related drugs, but not all. Carfentanil needed large amounts.
lines.but: These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff. The largest study reported no repeat tests.
how: One lab tested 28 related drugs on four brands. At high amounts, 21 to 24 of them showed up.
At lower amounts, only 5 to 12 of the 23 tested showed up.
Three never showed up on any brand. Carfentanil showed only at high amounts, and never on one brand.
A second lab found 11 of 13 related drugs on all five batches of one brand. On two of the three newer batches, carfentanil showed only in very large amounts.

card.statement: Fentanyl test strips can miss some drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil.
card.why: In lab tests of 28 related drugs on four brands, three never showed up on any brand, and carfentanil showed only at high amounts. These were mostly pure drugs in water, tested by lab staff.

lines.short: In small trials, MDMA's side effects were common and brief, and none were serious.
lines.but: These trials were too small to show rare or later harms.
how: Five small studies gave MDMA to 58 people. They had anxiety, depression, social anxiety with autism, or PTSD in couples.
A tight jaw, thirst, sweating and headache were common during sessions. Tiredness was common in the week after.
Blood pressure, pulse and body heat went up during sessions. None of this needed treatment.
Thoughts of suicide were recorded as side effects in a few people; in one trial this was as common with the dummy pill.

card.statement: In small MDMA trials, tiredness was common in the week after a session.
card.why: Five small trials gave MDMA to 58 people with conditions like anxiety or depression; a tight jaw, thirst and sweating were common during sessions, and none of the side effects were serious. The trials were too small to show rare or later harms.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

card.statement: Fewer people call themselves atheists after a DMT 'being' encounter, and after drug-free 'God' encounters too.
card.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

lines.short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in a smoky sealed room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.
lines.but: One small lab test in a sealed room, mostly in thick smoke; everyday smoke wasn't tested.
how: In a sealed room about 3 by 4 metres, 6 people smoked cannabis freely for an hour. 6 people who didn't smoke sat between them. This was done 3 times, each time with 6 new people sitting in: 18 in all.
Only 1 of 250 urine samples went over the US government's workplace limit. It did so on just 1 of 5 labs' tests.
Some private tests use a lower limit. There, 12 of the 18 tested positive at least once on at least one of 4 tests. A lab check would have confirmed it for 3 to 7, depending on the test.
A positive is a urine result: a THC breakdown product above a set level. It is not a measure of being high.

card.statement: Other people's cannabis smoke can never make you fail a urine drug test.
card.why: After an hour in a sealed, smoky room, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over the US government's workplace limit, and 12 tested positive at least once at a lower limit some private tests use. That was one small lab test, mostly in thick smoke, not everyday smoke.

lines.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
lines.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.

card.statement: In lab tests, fentanyl test strips often missed fentanyl that was really there.
card.why: Strips showed fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples that had it. But trained lab staff did the tests, mostly with one brand, and testing at home wasn't studied.

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

card.statement: In older US surveys, about 9 in 100 people who ever tried cannabis became dependent.
card.why: In the first survey, that was fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol. The surveys ran from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition; newer US figures that count milder cases are higher.

lines.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
lines.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.

card.statement: If a friend took the same MDMA and didn't overheat, you won't either.
card.why: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others: in one case of severe overheating, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat. That's second-hand, from one review of small studies and cases.

lines.short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.
lines.but: This is the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work, not from counts of people.
how: Lower risk, the review says: SSRI-type antidepressants and a few painkillers and cough medicines, which it says weaken ecstasy's effects.
Middle: stimulants such as amphetamine and cocaine, and supplements such as tryptophan. Highest: MAOI antidepressants.
Deaths from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy alone are rare, the review says, but harm is more likely with other drugs that act on serotonin.
No study counted how often each mix causes harm. Some people feel little from an amount of ecstasy and take more; no study measured what that does to the risk.

card.statement: All antidepressants carry about the same serotonin risk when mixed with ecstasy.
card.why: One 2007 review ranked MAOI antidepressants highest and SSRI-type antidepressants lower. That's the authors' judgment from reports and how the drugs work; no study counted how often each mix causes harm.

lines.short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.
lines.but: The scores are one panel's views, not measures, and alcohol's top score partly reflects how many people drink.
how: In 2010, experts scored 20 drugs on 16 harms in one day. A 2007 expert ranking put legal alcohol and tobacco above LSD and ecstasy.
Alcohol scored 72 of 100, 46 of them for harm to others. Critics say one score mixes harm per person with how many people use.
Tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose. Lung cancer was counted elsewhere. The authors agreed it probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined.
In an online survey, 1,501 people rated drug harms much like experts did. Of the 603 allowed to rate heroin, 467 had never used it.

card.statement: In a UK expert ranking of 20 drugs, tobacco scored zero for deaths like overdose.
card.why: Lung cancer was counted elsewhere, and the authors agreed tobacco probably kills more than the other 19 drugs combined. The scores are one panel's views, not measures.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

card.statement: In lab tests, men told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in it.
card.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

card.statement: Colour test kits for MDMA are easy to read, even for first-timers.
card.why: In one small 2003 lab study, two people new to the kit made many mistakes: one missed both MDMA samples, and the other called four other drugs MDMA. Lab experts got MDMA right.

lines.short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.
lines.but: Only a small one-week trial used just magic mushrooms; the bigger one was mostly LSD, and neither lasted months.
how: In Argentina, 34 people took magic mushroom capsules one week and look-alike capsules of an ordinary mushroom another. Mood and creativity did not improve.
A bigger study: 240 people mixed their own microdoses, mostly LSD, with empty capsules. After 4 weeks, the dummy group was not clearly worse off.
People guessed right about 7 times in 10. Ratings followed what they believed they took, though feeling an effect may have shaped the belief.
Everyone in both studies took capsules, so neither can show it is all placebo. People might have got better anyway.

card.statement: People who microdose can't tell a real microdose from a dummy capsule.
card.why: In trials, people guessed right about 7 times in 10, and their ratings followed what they believed they'd taken. Feeling an effect may have shaped that belief.

lines.short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.
lines.but: A positive test does not prove cause. A negative test may miss earlier use.
how: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to mephedrone; 13 results were still pending.
Of 62 deaths studied, mephedrone was the only substance found in 8. Other drugs were common.
One person died weeks later in hospital and had none found after death. Their earlier test evidence is not given.
The authors say tests and incomplete reporting may also miss deaths. They cannot give a death rate.

card.statement: When deaths were blamed on mephedrone, tests always found the drug in the body.
card.why: By October 2011, 128 deaths in the UK and nearby islands had been linked to it, and tests after death found none in 25. A negative test may miss earlier use, and a positive one doesn't prove cause.

lines.short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.
lines.but: The matching studies cover three places. The newest linked data are from 2012.
how: Some lists count drug poisoning as the main cause. Others count drugs found in tests, with age limits.
One death can be counted under several drugs. Finding a drug does not by itself show that it caused the death.
About 49 out of 100 people were on both lists in Norway. Fewer than half were on both in Sweden.
In New Mexico, about 89 out of 100 were on both lists. This study included other poisons too.

card.statement: There's one agreed way to count a death as a drug death.
card.why: Lists use different rules, some counting drug poisoning as the main cause and others drugs found in tests. In Norway, only about 49 in 100 deaths were on both of two lists, and in Sweden fewer than half.

lines.short: Bupropion and modafinil did not help more people stop than a dummy pill.
lines.but: The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm cannot be ruled out.
how: Putting five trials together: about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, on medicine or on a dummy pill.
The trials were small and uneven, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.
A later review of bupropion found about a tenth fewer positive urine tests. This result is uncertain.

card.statement: Bupropion and modafinil have been shown to help people stop using meth.
card.why: Across five trials, about 1 in 5 had stopped by the end, whether on medicine or a dummy pill. The trials were small, so a modest benefit or harm can't be ruled out.

lines.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.

card.statement: Ketamine trip reports read more like near-death accounts than those for any other drug.
card.why: In one study, a computer compared the words in about 15,000 online reports on 165 drugs with 625 near-death accounts, and ketamine's came out closest, with salvia and LSD close behind. Only words were compared, though: nobody showed the experiences themselves feel alike.

lines.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
lines.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.

card.statement: MDMA therapy papers left out side effects that their own trial records listed.
card.why: More than half of the less serious problems in the trial records never made it into the papers, and neither did 4 of 13 serious ones, all 4 in people on MDMA. Most studies also noted only problems people raised themselves.

lines.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as others. The studies checked from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.

card.statement: Kids who had the original DARE classes used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs less than kids who didn't.
card.why: Across 11 studies, kids who had the original classes said they used alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs about as much as kids who didn't. DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that newer version wasn't part of this review.

lines.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
lines.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.

card.statement: Most people who start using cocaine are hooked within a year.
card.why: In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had used only powder were dependent within a year of starting, and about 22 in 100 of those who went on to crack. People answered once, so the surveys can't show crack itself made the difference.

lines.short: Yes, among people who got ill: 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men, in one poison-centre study.
lines.but: It counts only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.
how: Only 188 of 545 people in California poison-centre records had a blood salt test. Of 105 women tested, 55 had a low level; of 83 men, 18 did.
Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma than women without one; in men the numbers were too small to tell.
A UK group (10 of 17 were women) and a review of published cases (more than 85 in 100 were female) point the same way, but the review's cases overlap with the California ones.
A review describes 8 women and 8 men given the same MDMA amount: a marker of a water-holding hormone rose only in women, with no clear difference reported in the hormone or blood salt.

card.statement: Among people who got ill after MDMA, low blood salt was more common in women than men.
card.why: In one poison-centre study, 52 in 100 women tested had low blood salt, against 22 in 100 men. It counted only people ill enough to be reported and tested, so it can't say who's most at risk among everyone who takes MDMA.

lines.short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.
lines.but: The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.
how: Researchers combined trials. People with long-lasting pain got a cannabis medicine or a dummy medicine (placebo).
Pain scores were about half a point lower out of 10 with the medicine.
37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%; this difference may be due to chance.
Most of the combined trials tested a mouth spray with THC and CBD, and none lasted more than 15 weeks.

card.statement: Cannabis medicines work much better than a dummy medicine for long-lasting pain.
card.why: In combined trials, pain was only about half a point lower out of 10 than with a dummy medicine. The trials were short, mostly tested one mouth spray, and many had weaknesses.

lines.short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.
lines.but: These studies can't show that cannabis caused it; other differences between the teens may explain it.
how: Seven long-term studies followed teens who did and did not use cannabis until they were young adults.
Teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. The studies did not say how many in 100 became depressed.
The studies took into account how depressed or anxious the teens were at the start, but not always tobacco or other drugs.
Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only three studies measured it.

card.statement: Teens who use the most cannabis are a bit more likely to be depressed as young adults.
card.why: Across seven long-term studies, teens in the highest-use group had about 1.4 times the odds of depression as young adults. That's a link, not proof: other differences between the teens may explain it.

lines.short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.
lines.but: Nobody in these studies was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.
how: The marker sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells in the brain.
Four teams used the same scan and all found less of it in the outer brain.
Deeper parts of the brain mostly looked the same as in other people.
Less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone.

card.statement: Brain scans prove that ecstasy destroys serotonin nerve cells.
card.why: Four teams found less of a serotonin marker in the outer brain of people who use ecstasy, but less marker can also mean cells make less of it, not that cells are gone. Nobody was scanned before they started, and these groups also used more other drugs.

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

card.statement: A psychedelic flashback means reliving the whole trip for hours.
card.why: In Swiss lab studies of LSD and psilocybin, a flashback was usually a few seconds of changed seeing, mostly in the days after, and most people didn't mind it. These were healthy, screened volunteers, with no drug-free group to compare.

lines.short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.
lines.but: Each was tested once in 14 to 16 healthy people, and the results come second-hand from a 2022 review.
how: Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, did not change heart rate or blood pressure. It lowered well-being by about 31 percent and raised anxiety by about 47 percent.
Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rise in heart rate by about 79 percent.
The review found no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA.
A slow start, as with methylphenidate, can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. No trial tested what happens then.

card.statement: Only a few psychiatric medicines have been tested together with MDMA in studies.
card.why: Each was tested once, in 14 to 16 healthy people, and results differed: with MDMA, the antipsychotic haloperidol lowered well-being and raised anxiety. For several others, a 2022 review found no controlled study at all.

lines.short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.
lines.but: No study compared how often people who use ketamine and people who don't get these problems. So none can show ketamine caused them.
how: In over 4,000 patients seen by doctors, mostly in Asia, about 77 in 100 needed to pee often and 60 in 100 had bladder pain.
In about 3 in 10 of these patients, urine had backed up and swollen a kidney. About 8 in 100 had weaker kidney function.
The survey was online, mostly in the UK: 1,285 people who had used ketamine in the past year. Those who used more reported more symptoms.
Of 251 people who described how symptoms changed, 128 said they eased after stopping. No study compared people who stopped with those who kept using.

card.statement: Bladder problems linked to ketamine never ease, even after people stop using it.
card.why: In one survey, 128 of 251 people who described how their symptoms changed said they eased after stopping. No study has compared people who stopped with people who kept using, though.

lines.short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
lines.but: It is a computer estimate, not a count. It applies risks from studies of groups of people to every country.
how: Researchers combined how much people drink in each country with cancer risks from earlier studies. They compared this with a world where no one had ever drunk.
They estimated 741,000 new cancers in 2020: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer made up the most.
Most were linked to more than 20 g of alcohol a day, about two drinks. About 103,000 were linked to less than that.
The model counted only harms, for the cancers an international agency lists. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths from alcohol in 2004.

card.statement: Drinking alcohol was estimated to cause about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.
card.why: A model put it at 741,000 new cancers, about 6 in 100 in men and 2 in 100 in women, led by gullet, liver, breast and bowel cancer. It's a computer estimate built on risks from studies of groups, not a count.

lines.short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.
lines.but: These studies only watched people, and gene studies found no sign that coffee itself lowers the risk of dying.
how: A big review gathered the research on coffee and health. Most of it came from studies that followed people for years.
People who drank coffee had lower rates of death, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and, most of all, liver disease.
In pregnancy, more coffee was linked to low birth weight and losing the pregnancy. Women who drank more had more fractures; men had fewer.
A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked; people who smoke tend to drink more coffee.

card.statement: Drinking coffee raises your risk of lung cancer.
card.why: A link between coffee and lung cancer disappeared in people who had never smoked: people who smoke tend to drink more coffee. These studies only watched people.

lines.short: Without their usual caffeine, half got a headache by evening; people given caffeine pills did not.
lines.but: Only 40 hospital patients took part, and surgery itself can also cause headaches.
how: 40 people who drank lots of caffeine had to stop it before a small operation.
Half got caffeine pills and half got identical dummy pills, and neither the patients nor the doctor checking symptoms knew which.
By evening, 10 of the 20 with dummy pills had a headache, and none with caffeine.

card.statement: Headaches from skipping caffeine come from expecting them, not from the missing caffeine.
card.why: Off their usual caffeine before a small operation, 10 of 20 people on dummy pills had a headache by evening and none of 20 on caffeine pills did, and neither they nor the doctor checking knew who got which. Only 40 patients took part, though, and surgery can also cause headaches.

lines.short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.
lines.but: Many mothers also smoked or drank. Most studies could not tell this apart from cannabis.
how: Researchers combined 19 studies, mostly from before 2000. They compared babies of mothers who did and did not use cannabis while pregnant.
Babies of mothers who used cannabis weighed about 109 grams less. More of them went to newborn intensive care.
It is not clear whether they were born early more often. Birth defects and deaths around birth were not clearly more common.
Most studies did not keep tobacco and alcohol apart from cannabis. So they cannot show that cannabis caused the differences.

card.statement: Babies whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy went to newborn intensive care more often.
card.why: Across 19 studies, mostly from before 2000, these babies were also about 109 grams lighter. But many mothers also smoked or drank, and most studies couldn't tell that apart from cannabis.

lines.short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.
lines.but: Testing for kratom varied and was not recorded, so some deaths with kratom were probably missed.
how: A CDC system gathered 27,338 overdose deaths from 27 US states, July 2016 to December 2017. Kratom was found in 152.
Kratom was named as a cause in 91 deaths. Other drugs turned up in 84 of them; fentanyl was named as a cause in 51.
Only 7 deaths had kratom as the only drug found. Even then, the report says other drugs cannot be ruled out.
The system counts mostly deaths where opioids played a part. With no count of people who use kratom, there is no death rate.

card.statement: Kratom shows up in a large share of US overdose deaths.
card.why: In 27 US states in 2016–17, kratom was found in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths, about 6 in 1,000. Testing for kratom varied and wasn't recorded, so some deaths with it were probably missed.

lines.short: Psychotic symptoms are more common in people who use meth, most of all in those who use it often.
lines.but: No study has settled which comes first.
how: In studies mostly in treatment, hospitals or prisons, a meth or amphetamine use disorder went with about 2.5 times the odds of psychosis.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth: use went with slightly more psychotic experiences.
In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years. Among people with no drug record, it was under 1 in 100.
None of these studies shows which came first.

card.statement: Most people who use meth end up diagnosed with psychosis.
card.why: In Taiwan, an estimated 4 in 100 adults arrested for using amphetamine-type drugs got a psychosis diagnosis within 10 years, against under 1 in 100 with no drug record. No study has settled which comes first.

lines.short: Yes. In the first week out, the risk of dying was about 1.5 to 2 times that of later weeks. Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause.
lines.but: It's death records only: they don't name the drugs, and nobody measured tolerance, so the study can't say why.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail in eight countries, between 1980 and 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause, in that first week and overall. Yet 91 in 100 of those deaths came after week 4, since people were followed for much longer than that.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.

card.statement: The risk of dying is highest in the first week after leaving prison.
card.why: In death records of about 1.5 million people, days 2 to 7 after release carried about 1.5 to 2 times the risk of later weeks, and drug or alcohol poisoning was the top recorded cause. Tolerance was never measured, so the records can't say why.

lines.short: Yes, if there's at least as much xylazine as they're made to find: 37 of 38 such samples read positive. With less, only 6 of 28 did.
lines.but: It's one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment, not powders or pills.
how: A lab tested 100 residue samples wiped from used syringes, bags and pill bottles, and checked them with a lab machine.
With enough xylazine, 37 of 38 read positive; with less, 6 of 28. That's 43 of all 66 with xylazine. None of 34 without it read positive.
In pure water, every strip read positive only from 2.5 times the amount the strip is made to find.
Lidocaine, a common cutting agent, also made strips read positive. At the one level tested, they didn't react to medetomidine. That's a similar drug used on animals.

card.statement: A negative xylazine test strip means there's no xylazine.
card.why: With less xylazine than strips are made to find, only 6 of 28 samples read positive, against 37 of 38 with at least that much. That was one batch of strips, read in a lab, on residues from used equipment.

lines.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
lines.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.

card.statement: A trial showed psilocybin works better than an antidepressant for depression.
card.why: In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression at 6 weeks or 6 months, even though people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin. But the trial was too small to show the two work equally well.

lines.short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.
lines.but: One test of products bought online in 2016; products sold in shops, or today, may differ.
how: CBD is a substance from the cannabis plant. Researchers bought every CBD oil, tincture and vape liquid with a CBD label they found online.
A lab that did not know the labels tested them. 36 held more CBD than the label said, and 22 held less.
Vape liquids were most often wrong: 21 of 24 were off by more than a tenth, mostly holding more CBD than labelled.
No one took the products, and no urine was tested. So this can't say if they cause a high or a positive drug test.

card.statement: CBD products usually contain what their labels say.
card.why: In a 2016 US test of 84 CBD products sold online, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label, and about 1 in 5 also held THC. Shop products, or today's, may differ.

lines.short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.
lines.but: Studies can't show that starting young is the cause. Much of the link runs in families.
how: A 1992 US survey asked adults who had used drugs at least 12 times. About 1 in 3 who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs. For those who started at 21 or older, it was about 1 in 7.

In New Zealand, children were asked about drinking and drugs at 13 and 15, not years later. At 32, 29 in 100 of those who used several times by 15, mostly alcohol, were dependent on alcohol or drugs. For teens with similar childhoods who had not, it was 15 in 100.
In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often had drug problems by the study's rules. It was about 48 in 100, against 33 in 100 for the other twin.
A bigger twin study found the link was not strong, and much of it ran in families. Its authors think waiting longer to start would cut the risk only a little.

card.statement: People who started using drugs at 13 or younger more often became dependent than later starters.
card.why: In a US survey of adults who'd used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started by 13 had been dependent, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older. A big twin study found much of the link runs in families, so starting young isn't shown to be the cause.

lines.short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.
lines.but: Only three small, old trials, mostly in hospital, and none with people coming off fentanyl.
how: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
Bad withdrawal happened to about 19 in 100 on the medicine and about 59 in 100 on the dummy pill.
About 56 in 100 finished treatment on the medicine, against 29 in 100 on the dummy pill.
The medicine made some people sleepy or dizzy and lowered their blood pressure.

card.statement: Clonidine and lofexidine barely help with heroin withdrawal.
card.why: In three trials, about 19 in 100 on them had bad withdrawal, against about 59 in 100 on a dummy pill, and more finished treatment. But the trials were small and old, and none included people coming off fentanyl.

lines.short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.
lines.but: Only 28 healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most, and no one was given more MDMA.
how: 16 volunteers rated MDMA's effects about 60 percent lower after citalopram; their blood levels were not measured.
In 12 men, paroxetine lessened the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size. Yet the MDMA peak in the blood was about 1 in 6 higher.
Feeling little can have many reasons: a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here.
No one was given more MDMA once its effects were muted, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk.

card.statement: An SSRI antidepressant that dulls MDMA's effects also lowers MDMA levels in your blood.
card.why: In 12 men, the SSRI paroxetine lessened MDMA's rises in blood pressure, heart rate and pupil size, yet the MDMA peak in their blood was about 1 in 6 higher. Only healthy volunteers were tested, for a few days at most.

lines.short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.
lines.but: The 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the counts do not show how common any mix is.
how: In 14,682 coroners' cases (2002 to 2008), 106 had MDMA in the blood. Six in 10 of them died of injuries such as hanging or a crash, so MDMA in the blood does not show that it caused the death.
The authors rated 19 of the 106 as having a risky drug combination. Of those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine (benzo).
Four of them had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type. Three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died.

A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.
