card.statement: When MDMA is found in the blood of someone who died, it usually caused the death.
card.why: In 106 Australian coroners' cases with MDMA in the blood, 6 in 10 died of injuries, such as a crash. A blood test after death can't show who took what, when or why.

lines.short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.
lines.but: Small hospital studies of 8 and 6 people. None measured heart attacks or rhythm problems.
how: Eight adults who already used both drugs took cocaine by the nose on a hospital ward. With alcohol, their heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute, against 74 with cocaine alone.
There was also about 13 to 15 percent more cocaine in their blood, and cocaethylene, which the body makes only when both drugs are there and which leaves the blood more slowly than cocaine.

In a second study, cocaine went into a vein with alcohol. Cocaethylene formed again, but stayed at a small fraction of the cocaine level, and none of it appeared when cocaine was given without alcohol.

Cocaethylene has been found in people's blood after both drugs, including after deaths, but such tests cannot show what caused a death. In over 1,000 emergency-room tests, people positive for both drugs had no more heart problems than people positive for one.

card.statement: Cocaine with alcohol makes the heart beat faster than cocaine alone.
card.why: In 8 people on a hospital ward, heart rate averaged about 84 beats a minute with both, against 74 with cocaine alone. These small studies didn't measure heart attacks or rhythm problems.

lines.short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.
lines.but: One small lab study from 2003, with a kit and pills of that time.
how: Three lab experts read all 35 samples with MDMA as positive, and nearly all of the 4 without MDMA as negative.
Seven MDMA samples also had another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine. The colour looked the same.
Two people new to the kit tested 8 known drugs. One missed both MDMA samples. The other called four other drugs MDMA.
A review says MDA and MDEA, drugs close to MDMA, give a similar colour. It adds that, read by eye, the tests do not show how much MDMA a pill holds.

card.statement: If a colour test shows MDMA, the pill has nothing else in it.
card.why: In one small 2003 lab study, seven MDMA samples that also held another drug, like caffeine or amphetamine, gave the same colour as MDMA alone. A review adds that drugs close to MDMA, like MDA, give a similar colour.

lines.short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.
lines.but: The studies were small, so small or moderate harm can't be ruled out. Binges were not tested.
how: Lab studies gave people mostly single doses.
Attention, memory and reaction time did not get measurably worse. On some tasks people did better.
The studies were small. The two main ones, and the review of the others, came from one research group.
Binges and long-term use were not tested.

card.statement: In lab studies, meth made attention and memory clearly worse at the time.
card.why: In small lab studies, attention, memory and reaction time didn't get measurably worse. But small or moderate harm can't be ruled out, and binges weren't tested.

lines.short: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, benzo prescriptions were linked to more poisoning deaths.
lines.but: The study did not take mental health, alcohol or street drug use into account.
how: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people per year with a benzo prescription, and 1 in 200 without.
The link was stronger when benzo doses were above the highest dose the UK drug guide advises.
Sleeping tablets called z-drugs were also linked to poisoning deaths, though deaths were few.
People prescribed benzos stayed in treatment longer, but the link with poisoning deaths was still there.

card.statement: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, people also prescribed benzos died of poisoning more often.
card.why: Poisoning deaths were about 1 in 100 people a year with a benzo prescription, against 1 in 200 without, even though those on benzos stayed in treatment longer. The study didn't allow for mental health, alcohol or street drug use.

lines.short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.
lines.but: Most people in the trials were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.
how: Naltrexone is a tablet. Dozens of trials gave it or dummy pills, mostly for 3 months, usually with counselling as well.
About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills. It helped less, if at all, with stopping completely.
People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100. Feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common.
When compared directly, naltrexone and acamprosate did about the same, but most people in that comparison were in one trial.

card.statement: Fewer people went back to heavy drinking on naltrexone than on dummy pills.
card.why: About 46 in 100 on naltrexone went back to heavy drinking, against 54 in 100 on dummy pills; feeling sick, dizziness and vomiting were more common. Most were middle-aged men who had already stopped drinking and had counselling.

lines.short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.
lines.but: The trials were from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.
how: Benzodiazepines are calming medicines. Old trials gave them or dummy pills to people going through alcohol withdrawal.
About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills. Delirium was also less common: about 2 in 100 against 6.
Other medicines were not clearly better or worse. One kind of antipsychotic given on its own was followed by more seizures and delirium than benzodiazepines.
Few trials looked at people who already had the DTs.

card.statement: In old trials, benzodiazepines made seizures during alcohol withdrawal much rarer.
card.why: About 1 in 100 people on a benzodiazepine had a seizure, against about 8 in 100 on dummy pills, and delirium was less common too. The trials ran from the 1960s to 1983, and few people had seizures.

lines.short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.
lines.but: Only ten people took part, and everyone could tell when they had been given a drug.
how: Ten healthy people had the S form, the R form and a dummy, a month apart.
On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.
The ordinary mix of the two forms was never given to these same ten people.

card.statement: Ketamine's two mirror-image forms, S and R, have the same effects.
card.why: In one study of ten healthy people, the S form raised scores for hallucinations and a changed sense of self in all ten, while the R form brought relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug.

On the S form, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self.
On the R form, the same people described relaxation, and their brain scans moved the other way.

card.why: In one study of ten healthy people, all ten scored higher for hallucinations and a changed sense of self on the S form, while on the R form they described relaxation. Everyone could tell when they'd been given a drug, though.

lines.short: A few small changes, some better and some worse, which may just be chance.
lines.but: One study of 24 people after one small lab dose; this report gives no mood or sleep data.
how: People took LSD on one day and a dummy drink (placebo) on another, in random order.
The next morning, a few memory and word tests went a little better after LSD.
One card-sorting puzzle about switching rules went a little worse after LSD.
The researchers checked many scores without allowing for that, so some differences may be luck.

card.statement: In a lab study, people's thinking was clearly worse the day after LSD.
card.why: In 24 people, a few memory and word tests went a little better the next morning and one rule-switching puzzle a little worse, which may just be chance. The report gave no mood or sleep data.

lines.short: People who use meth report low mood somewhat more often than people who don't.
lines.but: Other differences, such as using other drugs or a hard life, may explain part of it: against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference.
how: Across 6 studies, after allowing for some other differences, the odds of low mood were about 1.3 times higher.
Most studies measured symptoms, not diagnosed depression.
Two studies that followed people over time, allowing for how they felt before, found about 1.5 to 1.6 times the odds.
Among people who use other drugs, those who used meth did not report clearly more low mood.

card.statement: People who use meth report much more low mood than people who use other drugs.
card.why: Against people who use other drugs, there was no clear difference. Against people who don't use meth, low mood was somewhat more common, and things like a hard life may explain part of that.

lines.short: Among people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
lines.but: These were people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Not all of it is the drug.
how: In studies of people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.
That is nearly 7 times the rate of people of the same age and sex.
Overdose deaths were about 25 times as common; suicide and homicide about 12 times. These figures are less certain.
Many also used opioids or injected, so this does not show how much is due to the drug itself.

card.statement: People with regular or problematic meth or amphetamine use died nearly 7 times as often as others their age.
card.why: That's about 1 in 90 a year, in studies of people in treatment, in hospital or justice records, or who inject, not everyone who uses. Many also used opioids, so not all of it is the drug.

lines.short: Two long-term studies linked meth use to more violence. This held after other things were counted.
lines.but: Both studies share authors, and neither could show which came first.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became unclear once other things were counted.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth reported somewhat more violence in times they used meth or speed. This held after other things were counted.
In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth reported violent crime in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 without.
That study compared each person with themselves. But people reported use and crime for the same months.

card.statement: In one study, people dependent on meth reported more violent crime in months they used it.
card.why: It was about 12 in 100 months with meth use, against 3 in 100 without, comparing each person with themselves. But use and crime were reported for the same months, so which came first is unclear.

lines.short: Children on methylphenidate had sleep problems recorded more often than children on a dummy pill.
lines.but: The review says how many times more often, not how many children out of 100.
how: A review combined 35 trials in children and teenagers with ADHD.
Trouble falling asleep was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine as with the dummy pill.
Who recorded sleep problems, and whether a questionnaire was used, changed how big the difference looked.
A drug company paid for the review, and two of the authors work for its parent company.

card.statement: Children on the ADHD medicine methylphenidate had trouble falling asleep far more often than on a dummy pill.
card.why: Across 35 trials, it was recorded nearly three times as often with the medicine, though who recorded it changed how big the gap looked. A drug company paid for the review.

lines.short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.
lines.but: Each review used its own rules for what counts as a heroin death.
how: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine. Some death records said morphine or mixed drugs instead of heroin.
In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 52 in 100 of the deaths a fuller review linked to heroin.

In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), about 34 in 100 deaths a review linked to heroin lacked the heroin code in national figures. A few deaths coded as heroin were judged to involve it only by chance.
In England and Wales, an estimate came out about half as large again as the official count. It mixed heroin with morphine and did not match each death.

card.statement: A death record can say morphine even when the person took heroin.
card.why: In the body, heroin quickly turns into morphine, and some death records named morphine or mixed drugs instead. In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than the records did.

lines.short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye.
lines.but: These are uncontrolled reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot prove poppers were the cause, or show how often it happens or which poppers do it.
how: Doctors in at least 12 countries have written about 113 people with eye problems after poppers, some after using them once.
Most had both eyes affected: blurry or dim vision in the middle, flashes of light, or a blank spot.
In most people scanned, the scans showed damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina, at the back of the eye.
Of the people who had a second scan, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing.

card.statement: Scans of people with vision problems after poppers mostly showed damaged light-sensing cells at the back of the eye.
card.why: People described blurry or dim vision in the middle; of those scanned again, about 6 in 10 showed the damage improving or clearing. These are reports of about 113 people, so they can't prove poppers caused it or show how often it happens.

lines.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive. The heart races, breathing speeds up, and people get very restless and upset. Some lose touch with reality.
lines.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital. Suicidal thoughts or acts showed up in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.

card.statement: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive, with a racing heart and fast breathing.
card.why: The body can also overheat, chest pain can happen, and some people lose touch with reality. That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.

lines.short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.
lines.but: Four deaths cannot give a rate, and all four also had other drugs in their blood or urine.
how: None of the four had been prescribed moclobemide. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs.
The authors thought it was serotonin syndrome, but its defining signs were not recorded. MDMA levels were about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes.
Reviews rank MDMA with this kind of antidepressant as the highest-risk mix they list. Nobody has counted people who took both and had no such outcome.
Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA and take more. No study measured what happens then with this antidepressant.

card.statement: Reviews rank MDMA with antidepressants like moclobemide as the riskiest mix they list.
card.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

card.why: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood, and pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs. Four deaths can't give a rate, and all four also had other drugs.

lines.short: People given cocaine with alcohol did not feel more drunk, and sometimes slightly less.
lines.but: This is second-hand from one review of small studies, and no one tested driving.
how: A review gathered 14 small laboratory studies. The four that asked how drunk people felt had 8 to 11 people each. Those studies have not been read here, so the figures are second-hand.
In three of the four, people said they felt a little less drunk with cocaine; in one, nothing changed. Two of the three falls were too small to be clear.
Cocaine also made some alcohol-affected test scores less poor, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about 10 percent lower.

Nobody asked other people how drunk someone looked, and no study tested driving. Of drivers who died in crashes, about 4 in 100 had both drugs in their blood, so the mix did not protect them from alcohol's effects.

card.statement: Cocaine cancels out alcohol, so someone who has had both isn't really drunk any more.
card.why: In small lab studies, known second-hand from one review, people felt only a little less drunk or no different, and blood alcohol stayed the same or was about a tenth lower. Nobody tested driving, and about 4 in 100 drivers who died in crashes had both drugs in their blood.

lines.short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.
lines.but: The surveys are from 1990 to 2005 and used a narrower definition than today's.
how: A US survey in 1990 to 1992 asked about 8,000 people aged 15 to 54 about drug use and dependence.
Of those who had ever used cannabis, even once, about 9 in 100 had been dependent at some point: fewer than for tobacco, heroin, cocaine or alcohol.
A second US survey, in 2001 to 2005, estimated about 9 in 100 over a lifetime; half of those who became dependent did so within about 5 years of first use.
Newer US figures are higher, about 3 in 10, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

card.statement: People who try weed are more likely to get hooked than people who try alcohol.
card.why: In an older US survey, about 9 in 100 people who had ever tried cannabis had been dependent at some point: fewer than for alcohol, tobacco, cocaine or heroin. Newer US figures are higher, but they count milder cases and only people who used in the past year.

lines.short: Smoked, THC peaks in the blood within minutes; eaten, it rises slowly over hours.
lines.but: Old, small lab studies of weak cannabis, described in one review.
how: After smoking, THC in the blood peaked within minutes and fell to low levels within 2 hours.
After eating, it peaked 1 to 6 hours later, at lower levels, and the effects started later and lasted longer.
THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly; in people who use often, it can be found for days to weeks.

After one cigarette the last positive urine test came about 1 to 4 days later on average, and cannabis was found for 67 and 93 days in two people who used heavily; a positive test does not show when or how much.

card.statement: A positive urine test for weed shows the person used it in the past few days.
card.why: THC is stored in body fat and leaves it slowly: in two people who had used heavily, urine tests found cannabis for 67 and 93 days. A positive test doesn't show when or how much someone used.

lines.short: These studies can't say if it's the truth. But after a retreat, beliefs shifted a bit, towards ideas like other worlds and a conscious universe. The shift was still there 6 months later.
lines.but: The main study had no comparison group, and only 122 of over 800 people answered every survey. Most already leaned that way.
how: People answered questions a week before a psychedelic retreat or ceremony, then 4 weeks and 6 months after. In the 122 who answered all three, belief in things like other worlds rose a little.
First-timers shifted more. In one exploratory analysis, the shift went with feeling in tune with the group, not clearly with how mystical or visual the trip felt.
In a trial in depression, beliefs shifted after psilocybin. They shifted a little after a standard antidepressant too, and the gap was too small to be sure of.

A survey asked 1,606 people who said a trip had changed their beliefs to look back, about 8 years on average. 26 in 100 recalled thinking plants could be conscious before, and 61 in 100 after. Superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

card.statement: Among people who say a trip changed their beliefs, most afterwards thought plants could be conscious.
card.why: In a survey of 1,606 such people, 26 in 100 recalled thinking so before the trip and 61 in 100 after. They were looking back about 8 years on average, and superstitions, like black cats bringing bad luck, didn't rise.

lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.

card.statement: In 2001 Portugal made it legal to have drugs for your own use.
card.why: Not legal: having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels instead of a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to between 5,000 and 5,500 a year.

card.statement: After Portugal decriminalised drugs in 2001, the share of adults using drugs in the past year barely changed.
card.why: Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100, but past-year use barely moved. Treatment and other help grew at the same time, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.

lines.short: Yes, in two trials. With the same therapy, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: In the trial that asked, most knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.
how: In two trials run for one sponsor, 194 adults with PTSD had up to three long sessions with MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same therapy.
Both groups improved a lot. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped about 9 to 12 points more with MDMA, on a scale of 0 to 80.
Counting everyone who started, 61 to 70 in 100 on MDMA no longer had PTSD at about 4 months, against 27 to 39 in 100 on the dummy pill.
Neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The trials report nothing after 4 months, and none we read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused talking therapy.

card.statement: MDMA with therapy has helped people with PTSD more than the same therapy with a dummy pill.
card.why: In two trials, 61 to 70 in 100 no longer had PTSD after MDMA, against 27 to 39 in 100 after a dummy pill. But in the trial that asked, most people knew which pill they'd had, so expectations may explain part of the gap.

lines.short: Often better than before: less low mood and stress, more wellbeing, in most studies that checked. Some people got headaches, usually for a day or two, or slept badly.
lines.but: Most studies had no blind dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause, and most were supported sessions, not recreational use.
how: A review gathered 48 studies of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, with 1,774 people in all. People answered the same questionnaires before, and again a day to a month after.
Most studies that checked (70 to 90 in 100) found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, mindfulness and closeness to others. None found mental health worse on average.
Of 25 studies that said they looked for problems, 14 found some: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then poor sleep, tension and exhaustion.
One person had severe anxiety, and one went back to using methamphetamine. Half the studies didn't say whether they looked for problems at all.

card.statement: In the days after a psychedelic like LSD or shrooms, people usually feel lower than before, like a comedown.
card.why: In most studies that checked, people reported less low mood and stress and more wellbeing a day to a month after, and none found mental health worse on average. Most were supported sessions with no dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause.

lines.short: It can be: two expert reviews warn of life-threatening seizures, but not how often. The only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
lines.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one gives no source for them.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier paper.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and can feel like the problem the pills were for. Sleeping pills stopped after even a few nights can bring back worse sleep for a while.

Both warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. One says severe reactions can also happen when cutting down slowly, and that many reports are anecdotes; the other gives no source for its warning.
The only count comes second-hand, from a 1961 study: 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.

card.statement: Stopping benzos such as Xanax or Valium suddenly can bring on seizures.
card.why: Two expert reviews warn that seizures after stopping suddenly can be life-threatening. They don't say how often: the only count they give is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.

lines.short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.
lines.but: Only one study, and people chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.
how: In Bristol, UK, 416 adults were asked to skip caffeine overnight. The next day, chance decided who got caffeine pills and who got dummy pills.
By the afternoon, people who often have caffeine but got dummy pills were the sleepiest and slowest. They made the most mistakes.
Caffeine brought them about level with people who rarely have it, no higher. In those people, caffeine raised jitters, not alertness.
Five people who often have caffeine quit the test day early. All five had dummy pills; four gave headache and feeling sick as reasons.

card.statement: In a lab test, people who often have caffeine were sleepier and slower without it than people who rarely do.
card.why: Skipping caffeine left them the sleepiest and slowest, and taking it only brought them level with people who rarely have it, no higher. People chose their own caffeine habits, so something else about them could explain it.

lines.short: Not necessarily. Older studies often found other drugs too: alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100 of these deaths. But finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.
lines.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours, and other people were often there: more than half the time, in four studies. These come second-hand, from a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classed 23 in 100 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners as something other than a direct overdose, like an infection, an injury, or drug effects plus an illness.
Heroin use can also be missed, because its marker can fall after death. Levels also depend on where and when samples are taken.

card.statement: Most people who die of a heroin overdose have no other drug in their body.
card.why: In older studies, no other drug was found in only 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose, and alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100. Finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.

lines.short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.
lines.but: People were asked once, so the survey can't show whether LSD, mushrooms or mescaline cause or prevent problems.
how: 130,152 US adults answered private computer questions at home in 2001 to 2004; 21,967 had ever used LSD, mushrooms, mescaline or peyote.
At first glance, all 20 mental health measures were 2 to 3 times as common in people who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline.

lines.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.

lines.short: Studies from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes after pure LSD. Early reports of more breaks came mostly from people using many drugs.

card.why: The 1967 scare began with LSD added to blood cells in a lab dish. When 32 patients were tested before and after pure LSD there was no clear rise in damaged cells, though these were small studies of blood cells only.

lines.short: Yes, some do. How many depends on who's asked: about 4 in 100 people who'd used it recently in US surveys, but up to 73 in 100 in small groups.

In one study, symptoms eased after a month of using a vaporizer instead of smoking, but it had no comparison group.

card.why: Of young children in US poison-centre calls about edibles, more than 1 in 5 were admitted to hospital and 35 needed a breathing tube; no deaths were reported. Such calls rose about 15 times over from 2017 to 2021.

Each form, from patches to sprays, did better than its own comparison.
These were people trying to stop, so the trials say nothing about anyone else.

The review's authors suggest, without data, that people whose effects were muted may have taken more.

card.statement: In safety reports about ecstasy, death was more common when the report also named an antidepressant.
card.why: In US reports, those cases had about 1.6 times the odds of a fatal outcome, and reports naming muscle relaxants or anesthetics had higher odds still. These are voluntary reports, so they can't show cause, and nobody knows how many people took each mix.

lines.short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.
lines.but: Other differences between people could explain it. Twin studies of lighter use found no clear extra loss.
how: In New Zealand, 874 people took IQ tests as children and again at 38.
The 38 people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups lost about 6 points from their childhood scores. People who never used gained a little.
Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern. The first team found that family background did not change their result.
In US and British twin studies, mostly of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more than the twin who did not. These studies could miss a small loss.

card.statement: In twin studies, the twin who used cannabis as a teen lost clearly more IQ than the other twin.
card.why: No clear extra loss, though these studies, mostly of lighter use, could miss a small one. One study found about 6 points lost after years of dependence.

lines.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
lines.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
It's not just DMT. Of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind. 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before the meeting, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.

card.statement: After meeting a 'being' on DMT, fewer people call themselves atheists. The same happens after drug-free 'God' encounters.
card.why: Among people who'd had such meetings, 28 in 100 recalled being atheists before a DMT encounter and 10 in 100 said they were now, and the share fell without drugs too. But they were recalling old beliefs years later.

lines.short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.
lines.but: Lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s; the drinking test lasted 15 minutes, with low blood alcohol.
how: 64 men were told at random that their drink had vodka or not, and were given vodka or not, also at random. Half had a history of drinking problems.
Men told it had vodka drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, whatever was really in the glass. Real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank.
Across 36 similar experiments, believing you had drunk alcohol went with more drinking, but not with changes in mood or memory. Sexual arousal rose on average, but that varied a lot between studies.
The alcohol itself, not the belief, affected memory, coordination, body sensations and mood. Blood alcohol in the drinking study stayed low, so heavier drinking may differ.

card.statement: In lab tests, men who were told their drink had vodka drank more, whatever was really in the glass.
card.why: They drank about twice as much in 15 minutes, while real vodka made no clear difference to how much they drank. These were lab tests from the 1970s and 1980s, with low blood alcohol.

lines.short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.
lines.but: Published cases only: nobody knows how common it is, and fewer than half were followed up.
how: A 2017 review pooled 211 published cases; all had bouts of vomiting with severe nausea, and most had belly pain.
About 3 in 4 used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before it started.
Most found that hot baths or showers eased it for a while, but many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too.
Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better; the 21 who kept using did not.

card.statement: Regular cannabis use can come with bouts of severe vomiting. In most reported cases, it ended when people stopped using.
card.why: Of 64 people whose stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better. Nobody knows how common it is.

lines.short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.
lines.but: This compared different studies, not the same people before and after they stopped.
how: A review of 69 studies found a smaller gap in studies that asked people to stop for more than 3 days. The gap might be zero, but one almost as big as the overall gap is not ruled out.
Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree. Some found lower scores on some tests; others found none.
Few studies followed people for longer. In one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not score differently on any test from people who had not used.
Two reviews read this evidence in opposite ways. Researchers disagree.

card.statement: A year or more after quitting heavy cannabis use, people in one study scored like people who hadn't used.
card.why: They scored no differently on any test, and a big review found smaller gaps in studies that asked people to stop for over 3 days. But few studies have followed people that long, and researchers disagree.

lines.short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.
lines.but: The people studied were healthy adults with low to moderate usual caffeine intake, so heavy users, teenagers and older adults may differ.
how: 24 studies compared nights after caffeine with nights without it, in the same people.
Caffeine made falling asleep slower, time awake in the night longer, and sleep lighter.
The more caffeine, and the closer to bedtime, the more sleep people lost.
In five studies, people did not report more time awake in the night.

card.statement: Caffeine kept people awake longer in the night, yet in five studies people didn't say they had been awake more.
card.why: Across 24 studies, caffeine made falling asleep slower and time awake longer; in five, people did not report more time awake.

lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.

Two months on, 19 of the 24 who answered said it had raised their wellbeing, against 5 after the stimulant. People close to them saw a small change for the better; personality and mood tests showed no difference.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.

card.statement: Most volunteers in one lab study ranked one session on psilocybin, the magic-mushroom drug, among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
card.why: Two months later, 67 in 100 did. But everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.

lines.short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.
lines.but: These were healthy, screened volunteers in labs, with no drug-free group to compare.
how: 142 healthy adults took LSD, psilocybin or both in lab studies in Switzerland.
At the end, 13 said they had had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.
Most did not mind it; 2 people were upset by it.
Nobody was found to have the long-lasting vision condition doctors call HPPD.

card.why: Of 142 healthy lab volunteers, 13 said they had a flashback, usually a few seconds of changed seeing.

lines.short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.
lines.but: Nobody has been scanned while using and then again years later.
how: Three studies compared different people and found more marker in those who stopped longer ago.
Two other studies found no link with time since the last pill.
People who stop may be different from people who keep going.
The parts that looked normal again are not where the drop is biggest.

card.statement: Scans show serotonin changes in people who used ecstasy, and these changes are known to be permanent.
card.why: Nobody knows: three studies found more of the scan marker in people who had stopped longer ago, two found no link with time, and no one has been scanned while using and again years later.

items.what: suggests the same studies were looked at again, which the lines do not say

lines.short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.
lines.but: These studies compare crashed drivers with others, so they cannot show one driver's chance of crashing.
how: Across 28 results from 21 studies in 13 countries, drivers with cannabis found in a test had about 1.2 to 1.4 times the odds of a crash, or of being at fault in one.
An older review found 1.9 times. Re-checking its counts and allowing for other factors brought the same studies to between 1.2 and 1.4.
Studies that allowed for alcohol found 1.1 to 1.2 times. Studies that did not found 1.7 to 1.8 times.
A positive test shows cannabis was in the body, not that a driver was impaired.

card.statement: Cannabis is linked to car crashes just as strongly once studies take drivers' drinking into account.
card.why: It shrinks: studies that allowed for alcohol found about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of a crash, against 1.7 to 1.8 in studies that didn't. These compare crashed drivers with others, so they can't show one driver's chance of crashing.
